title: VLM-based automatic multi-granularity graph representation of building layouts for design informatics
summary: Architectural floorplan images encode rich relational knowledge among functional spaces, which underpins design retrieval, knowledge-based reasoning, and BIM enrichment through the building lifecycle. However, it remains challenging to automatically construct task-adaptive graph representations for public buildings. To address this gap, we first define a multi-granularity Level-of-Graphs (LoGs) for public building layouts. Methodologically, we present a Vision-Language Model (VLM)-based automatic LoG construction through node identification, edge inference, text parsing, and graph coarsening. VLM-generated representations are systematically evaluated and tested in real-world tasks, using 147 academic library floorplans worldwide as a case study. Experiments showed VLM-generated graphs were broadly consistent with human-labeled graphs (matched node ratio >= 92%; 509.3 s per floor plan for three-LoG graph generation). Meso-grained graphs yield the best node-level zone prediction (Macro F1 = 0.647, at 65% of fine-grained complexity), while coarse-grained graphs are most effective for graph-level layout quality evaluation (Spearman's \r{ho} = 0.610, at 16% of fine-grained complexity). By enabling scalable, annotation-free extraction of structured layout information from floorplan images, this study advances design informatics by converting plan images into knowledge representations, thereby enhancing the utilization of design information across the building life cycle.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a Vision-Language Model-based automatic method for constructing multi-granularity graph representations (Level-of-Graphs) from architectural floorplan images, validated on 147 academic library floorplans. VLM-generated graphs achieve high consistency with human annotations (≥92% matched nodes) and demonstrate task-adaptive performance: meso-grained graphs excel at node-level zone prediction (Macro F1=0.647) while coarse-grained graphs are best for graph-level layout quality evaluation (Spearman's ρ=0.610), all at significantly lower computational complexity than fine-grained graphs.
AI.motivation: Architectural floorplans contain rich relational knowledge among functional spaces essential for design retrieval, knowledge-based reasoning, and BIM enrichment, but automatically constructing task-adaptive graph representations for public buildings remains challenging.
AI.method: The authors define a multi-granularity Level-of-Graphs (LoGs) framework for public building layouts, then present a VLM-based automatic LoG construction pipeline comprising four stages: node identification, edge inference, text parsing, and graph coarsening. The method is evaluated on 147 academic library floorplans worldwide.
AI.result: VLM-generated graphs achieved a matched node ratio ≥92% with human-labeled graphs, with a generation time of 509.3 seconds per floorplan for all three LoG levels. Meso-grained graphs delivered the best node-level zone prediction (Macro F1=0.647) at 65% of fine-grained complexity, while coarse-grained graphs excelled at graph-level layout quality evaluation (Spearman's ρ=0.610) at only 16% of fine-grained complexity.
AI.conclusion: The study enables scalable, annotation-free extraction of structured layout information from floorplan images, advancing design informatics by converting plan images into knowledge representations and enhancing utilization of design information across the building life cycle.

title: SIMGUIDE: Procedurally Grounded Multi-Context Representations for Personalized Agent Planning
summary: Personalized AI agents overwhelmingly treat users as single entities: a flat profile concatenated into a prompt. This fails when the same person holds different priorities across life contexts -- and fails catastrophically when those priorities conflict. The core problem is not that agents lack information about users; it is that the format of user representations determines whether an agent can act on that information at all. We introduce SIMGUIDE, a method that structures user context into typed, domain-specific blocks called Sims and grounds each constraint with procedural examples drawn from past decisions. To evaluate this, we construct SIMBENCH, a diagnostic suite of 47 preference-conditioned planning tasks where the correct plan depends on which user context is active -- a property no existing benchmark tests. Declarative Sim constraints alone do not outperform retrieval-based personalization (RAG). Procedurally grounded Sims outperform RAG on GPT-4o (+7.9 Preference Adherence points, $p = 0.013$), and this advantage replicates on 100 $τ$-bench tasks across both GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet~4.5 ($p \leq 0.023$). At the parametric level, the same principle holds: training distribution dominates whether parametric adaptation succeeds at all. Task-matched LoRA fine-tuning improves generation quality by 12.8 ROUGE-L points over the unadapted base model, and routing adapters by Sim type rather than user identity adds a further 7.3 points, robust to 28% routing error. Representation format -- not representation content -- is the first-order design variable.

AI.tldr: Personalized AI agents typically treat users as flat, single-entity profiles, failing when the same user holds conflicting priorities across different life contexts. SIMGUIDE structures user context into typed, domain-specific blocks ("Sims") grounded with procedural examples from past decisions, and SIMBENCH is a diagnostic suite of 47 preference-conditioned planning tasks. Procedurally grounded Sims outperform RAG personalization on GPT-4o and Claude across benchmarks, and parametric adaptation benefits from task-matched fine-tuning and Sim-type-based adapter routing.
AI.motivation: The core problem is not insufficient user information but the format of user representations: flat, concatenated profiles prevent agents from acting on contextual preferences. When the same person holds conflicting priorities across life contexts (e.g., work vs. home), a single flat representation is fundamentally inadequate. Existing benchmarks do not test whether the correct plan depends on which user context is active.
AI.method: SIMGUIDE represents user context as typed, domain-specific blocks called Sims, each grounded with procedural examples drawn from past decisions. The authors construct SIMBENCH, a suite of 47 preference-conditioned planning tasks where the correct plan is contingent on the active user context. They compare declarative Sims, procedurally grounded Sims, and RAG-based personalization. At the parametric level, they study LoRA fine-tuning with task-matched data and adapter routing by Sim type versus user identity, including robustness to routing error.
AI.result: Declarative Sim constraints alone do not outperform RAG. Procedurally grounded Sims outperform RAG by +7.9 Preference Adherence points on GPT-4o (p=0.013), replicating on 100 τ-bench tasks across GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet 4.5 (p ≤ 0.023). Task-matched LoRA fine-tuning improves generation quality by 12.8 ROUGE-L points over the unadapted base model, and Sim-type-based adapter routing adds a further 7.3 points, robust to 28% routing error.
AI.conclusion: Representation format — not representation content — is the first-order design variable in personalization. Structuring user context into typed, procedurally grounded blocks is more effective than either flat profiles or retrieval-based approaches, and this principle holds at both the inference/context level and the parametric/adaptation level.

title: Reliable LLM-Powered Decision Engines for Large-Scale Supply Chain Operations: Architecture, Safety, and Performance Guarantees
summary: Current large-scale supply chains are highly uncertain, dynamic, and disruption prone that are challenging to serve up timely and resilient decisions through traditional rule-based and optimization-only systems. The increasing supply of heterogeneous data sources, such as transactional demand signals and unstructured disruption report, presents a chance of intelligent systems, which could reason, adapt and optimize at the same time. A hybrid architecture that combines large language models (LLMs) with mathematical optimization, probabilistic forecasting, and safety-constrained decision filtering is proposed in this paper as a performance of a Decision Engine, which is called LLM-Powered Decision Engine (LLM-DE). In comparison to purely data-driven or heuristic solutions, LLM-DE integrates semantic reasoning with LLM with a set of performance and safety guarantees that allow safe decision-making in large-scale supply chain processes. The suggested framework enables the end-to-end decision making such as demand forecasting, inventory optimization, and transportation routing and disruption mitigation. The findings affirm that language-based reasoning combined with optimization and formal constraints can be used to come up with not only smarter but also safer and more scalable supply chain decisions. This research provides a new architecture, a complete pipeline of algorithm, and a formulation based on mathematical constructs of the operational decision systems incorporating LLM. The proposed model offers a pragmatic and theoretical basis of the next-generation intelligent supply chain infrastructures that can be implemented to work dependably in the face of uncertainty and massive complexity.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an LLM-Powered Decision Engine (LLM-DE), a hybrid architecture combining large language models with mathematical optimization, probabilistic forecasting, and safety-constrained decision filtering to enable safe, scalable, and resilient decision-making in large-scale supply chain operations.
AI.motivation: Traditional rule-based and optimization-only supply chain systems struggle to handle high uncertainty, dynamism, and disruptions. The growing availability of heterogeneous data sources (transactional signals and unstructured disruption reports) creates an opportunity for intelligent systems that can reason, adapt, and optimize simultaneously.
AI.method: The authors propose a hybrid Decision Engine (LLM-DE) that integrates LLM-based semantic reasoning with mathematical optimization, probabilistic forecasting, and safety-constrained decision filtering. The framework supports end-to-end decision-making across demand forecasting, inventory optimization, transportation routing, and disruption mitigation.
AI.result: The findings demonstrate that combining language-based reasoning with optimization and formal constraints yields supply chain decisions that are smarter, safer, and more scalable than purely data-driven or heuristic approaches.
AI.conclusion: The research contributes a new architecture, a complete algorithmic pipeline, and a mathematical formulation for operational decision systems incorporating LLMs, providing both a pragmatic and theoretical foundation for next-generation intelligent supply chain infrastructures that can operate reliably under uncertainty and large-scale complexity.

title: AI-Powered Mental Health Chatbots in Africa: A Systematic Review and Culturally Adaptive Framework
summary: Mental health challenges in Africa remain under-addressed due to inadequate infrastructure, stigma, and a chronic shortage of professionals. Artificial Intelligence (AI)-powered chatbots are emerging globally as low-cost, accessible tools that can offer psychological support. This paper presents a systematic review of 52 empirical studies published between 2017 and 2025, critically analysing their cultural, linguistic, and infrastructural relevance to African contexts. The findings demonstrate the potential of AI chatbots to improve accessibility, reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression, and expand psychosocial support, yet reveal limited African-specific adaptation. Most systems remain rooted in Western models and English-language designs, leaving critical gaps in local relevance, inclusivity, and sustainability. Based on the findings, the authors develop a Culturally Adaptive Digital Mental Health (CADMH) framework that integrates African cultural values, multilingual design, mobile-first optimisation, and ethical safeguards. The study highlights opportunities and barriers for integrating AI chatbots into African healthcare, offering guidance for research, practice, and policy.

AI.tldr: A systematic review of 52 empirical studies (2017–2025) on AI-powered mental health chatbots reveals their potential to improve accessibility and reduce anxiety/depression symptoms, but finds limited cultural, linguistic, and infrastructural adaptation for African contexts. The authors propose a Culturally Adaptive Digital Mental Health (CADMH) framework integrating African cultural values, multilingual design, mobile-first optimization, and ethical safeguards.
AI.motivation: Mental health challenges in Africa are under-addressed due to inadequate infrastructure, stigma, and a chronic shortage of professionals. AI-powered chatbots offer a potential low-cost, accessible solution, but their relevance and adaptability to African cultural, linguistic, and infrastructural contexts remain unclear.
AI.method: A systematic review of 52 empirical studies published between 2017 and 2025, critically analyzing their cultural, linguistic, and infrastructural relevance to African contexts.
AI.result: Findings demonstrate AI chatbots' potential to improve accessibility, reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression, and expand psychosocial support, yet reveal limited African-specific adaptation. Most systems remain rooted in Western models and English-language designs, leaving critical gaps in local relevance, inclusivity, and sustainability.
AI.conclusion: The authors develop a Culturally Adaptive Digital Mental Health (CADMH) framework that integrates African cultural values, multilingual design, mobile-first optimisation, and ethical safeguards. The study highlights opportunities and barriers for integrating AI chatbots into African healthcare, offering guidance for research, practice, and policy.

title: GaussVLA: Geometry-Aware Spatial Reasoning for Vision-Language-Action Model
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models encode visual observations as flat 2D patch tokens that carry no intrinsic geometric structure, and augmenting them with dense monocular depth injects per-pixel scalar values that encode neither surface orientation nor geometric confidence. This leaves the policy with limited structured spatial reasoning for action prediction. We propose GaussVLA, a Mamba-based VLA that incorporates two custom modules: Gaussian Spatial Tokenizer (GST) to lift frozen semantic and depth features into compact 3D Gaussian tokens, pools geometrically salient regions with learned queries, and \emph{Depth-Aware Chain-of-Thought (DA-CoT)} that performs structured, non-autoregressive geometric reasoning under language and flow-time conditioning. Across both simulation and real-world evaluations, GaussVLA demonstrates strong spatial-manipulation performance while remaining parameter-efficient. On LIBERO, it achieves 93.5% average success and 100.0% success on the Spatial suite with only 200M parameters, improving over SpatialVLA by 19.7% relative average success while remaining significantly more parameter-efficient.

AI.tldr: GaussVLA is a Mamba-based Vision-Language-Action model that lifts semantic and depth features into compact 3D Gaussian tokens (via a Gaussian Spatial Tokenizer) and performs non-autoregressive geometric reasoning (via Depth-Aware Chain-of-Thought). It achieves 93.5% average success on LIBERO with only 200M parameters, improving 19.7% relative over SpatialVLA on average success while being far more parameter-efficient.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA models encode visual observations as flat 2D patch tokens lacking intrinsic geometric structure, and dense monocular depth provides only per-pixel scalar values without surface orientation or geometric confidence. This limits the policy's structured spatial reasoning capability for action prediction.
AI.method: GaussVLA introduces two modules: (1) Gaussian Spatial Tokenizer (GST) that lifts frozen semantic and depth features into compact 3D Gaussian tokens and pools geometrically salient regions via learned queries; (2) Depth-Aware Chain-of-Thought (DA-CoT) that performs structured, non-autoregressive geometric reasoning conditioned on language and flow-time.
AI.result: On LIBERO, GaussVLA achieves 93.5% average success and 100.0% success on the Spatial suite with only 200M parameters, improving over SpatialVLA by 19.7% relative average success while remaining significantly more parameter-efficient. Strong performance is demonstrated in both simulation and real-world spatial-manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Embedding geometric structure directly into token representations and reasoning chains enables parameter-efficient VLA models to achieve strong spatial manipulation performance, outperforming prior methods with substantially fewer parameters.

title: Measurement-Budget Allocation in Quantum Learning with Finite-Shot Generalization Guarantees
summary: On near-term quantum hardware, estimating a Born probability requires repeated circuit executions. A quantum learning experiment with a fixed measurement budget $B$ must therefore decide how many distinct training states $n$ to use and how many shots $S$ to allocate to each state. We study this tradeoff for binary quantum classifiers with fixed or independently selected measurement operators $M$, where the ideal score is $\Tr(Mρ)$. We prove a distribution-free generalization bound that separates the finite-sample and finite-shot contributions. The sample term scales as $\sqrt{d/n}$, while the shot term scales as $\sqrt{(\log n)/S}$; under the constraint $B=nS$, these two terms move in opposite directions. Minimising a conservative closed-form surrogate of the bound gives the allocation rule $\nstar = 2\sqrt{2dB/\log(2B/δ)}$ and $\Sstar = B/\nstar$. This surrogate has the same asymptotic scaling as the exact minimizer and yields a worst-case rate of $B^{-1/4}$. The guarantee is intentionally conservative, since it applies to the full class of binary quantum measurements. We complement the theory with PennyLane simulations using 2-qubit and 4-qubit variational quantum circuits on nine synthetic binary classification benchmarks. In all tested configurations, the one-sided empirical generalization gap remains below the theoretical bound. The result provides a conservative statistical guideline for allocating measurement budgets in finite-shot evaluation and pre-experimental planning for near-term quantum learning systems, complementing hardware-level scheduling and circuit-design considerations. Extending the guarantee to fully adaptive shot-noisy training remains an open problem.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the tradeoff between the number of training states (n) and shots per state (S) in binary quantum classifiers with a fixed measurement budget B. The authors prove a distribution-free generalization bound separating finite-sample and finite-shot contributions (scaling as √(d/n) and √((log n)/S) respectively), derive an optimal allocation rule n* = 2√(2dB/log(2B/δ)) and S* = B/n*, achieving a worst-case rate of B^{-1/4}, and validate the theoretical bound with PennyLane simulations on 2-qubit and 4-qubit variational circuits across nine synthetic benchmarks.
AI.motivation: On near-term quantum hardware, estimating Born probabilities is expensive and requires repeated circuit executions. A quantum learning experiment with a fixed measurement budget must decide how to allocate that budget between the number of distinct training states and the number of shots per state—a fundamental tradeoff that has not been theoretically characterized for quantum classifiers.
AI.method: The authors prove a distribution-free generalization bound for binary quantum classifiers with fixed or independently selected measurement operators, separating the sample term (~√(d/n)) and shot term (~√((log n)/S)). They minimize a conservative closed-form surrogate under the constraint B = nS to derive the allocation rules n* and S*, and validate via PennyLane simulations with variational quantum circuits on nine synthetic classification benchmarks.
AI.result: The conservative surrogate yields the allocation rule n* = 2√(2dB/log(2B/δ)) and S* = B/n*, matching the asymptotic scaling of the exact minimizer and achieving a worst-case rate of B^{-1/4}. In all PennyLane simulations (2-qubit and 4-qubit variational circuits across nine benchmarks), the one-sided empirical generalization gap remains below the theoretical bound.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a conservative statistical guideline for allocating measurement budgets in finite-shot evaluation and pre-experimental planning for near-term quantum learning systems, complementing hardware-level scheduling and circuit-design considerations. Extending the guarantee to fully adaptive shot-noisy training remains an open problem.

title: ROS2 Connect: A new ROS2 over WAN Solution
comment: Proceedings of the 8th International Workshop on Robotics Software Engineering co-located with the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ROSE '26)
summary: The Robot Operating System 2 (ROS2) has become a widely adopted framework for the development of distributed robotic systems. However, its communication architecture, based on DDS and RTPS, relies on multicast discovery mechanisms that are typically unavailable in wide-area network (WAN) environments, making remote operation challenging. This work presents ROS2 Connect, a WebSocket-based communication framework that enables transparent and secure ROS2 interaction across routed networks without requiring modifications to network infrastructure or DDS configurations. The proposed client-server architecture supports bidirectional exchange of topics, services, actions, and system data while integrating authentication and access control mechanisms. Experimental evaluation over a real WAN connection demonstrates significantly lower latency, higher stability, and improved scalability compared to existing solutions, including DDS Router, rosbridge and Zenoh. Initial results show that ROS2 Connect provides a reliable foundation for teleoperation and distributed robotics applications over wide-area networks.

AI.tldr: ROS2 Connect is a WebSocket-based communication framework that enables transparent and secure ROS2 interaction across wide-area networks (WANs) without requiring changes to network infrastructure or DDS configurations. It supports bidirectional exchange of topics, services, actions, and system data with built-in authentication and access control. Experimental evaluation over a real WAN shows lower latency, higher stability, and improved scalability compared to DDS Router, rosbridge, and Zenoh.
AI.motivation: ROS2's communication architecture relies on DDS and RTPS multicast discovery mechanisms that are typically unavailable in WAN environments, making remote operation and distributed robotics over routed networks challenging.
AI.method: A client-server architecture based on WebSocket that supports transparent and secure bidirectional exchange of ROS2 topics, services, actions, and system data across routed networks, with integrated authentication and access control, without requiring network infrastructure or DDS configuration modifications.
AI.result: Experimental evaluation over a real WAN connection demonstrates significantly lower latency, higher stability, and improved scalability compared to existing solutions including DDS Router, rosbridge, and Zenoh.
AI.conclusion: ROS2 Connect provides a reliable foundation for teleoperation and distributed robotics applications over wide-area networks.

title: Natural Language Input, Semantic Track Representation, and LLM Inference: Making the Maritime Information Exchange Model Tractable
summary: We describe a practical architecture for making the Maritime Information Exchange Model (MIEM) and the broader Rich Semantic Track model tractable using current large language model (LLM) technology. The barrier to adoption of semantic track models in defense and law enforcement has been the requirement that operators learn formal ontology languages and manually encode observations as typed logical assertions. We propose eliminating this barrier entirely: operators contribute observations in natural language; an LLM translates these into typed Semantic Assertion Records (SARs), which are named case frames that capture n-ary relations in a single compact structure; a knowledge graph accumulates the SARs; and a second LLM pass performs inference, anomaly detection, and hypothesis ranking over the graph. We work through two detailed examples (a 9/11-era pre-attack indicator scenario and a maritime cargo inspection scenario) showing the full pipeline from natural language input to SAR representation to inference output. We argue that this architecture makes the Track Model and MIEM immediately deployable with current technology, establishes prior art against proprietary enclosure of the approach, and grounds the method in a theoretical framework connecting semantic track representations to neural manifold geometry.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a practical architecture that makes the Maritime Information Exchange Model (MIEM) and Rich Semantic Track model deployable using current LLM technology. It eliminates the barrier of operators needing to learn formal ontology languages by having LLMs translate natural language observations into typed Semantic Assertion Records (SARs), stored in a knowledge graph, with a second LLM pass performing inference, anomaly detection, and hypothesis ranking.
AI.motivation: The barrier to adoption of semantic track models in defense and law enforcement is that operators must learn formal ontology languages and manually encode observations as typed logical assertions. The authors propose removing this barrier entirely so that operators can contribute observations in natural language.
AI.method: The architecture uses LLMs to translate natural language observations into typed Semantic Assertion Records (SARs)—named case frames capturing n-ary relations in a single compact structure. SARs are accumulated in a knowledge graph, and a second LLM pass performs inference, anomaly detection, and hypothesis ranking over the graph.
AI.result: Two detailed examples are provided—a 9/11-era pre-attack indicator scenario and a maritime cargo inspection scenario—demonstrating the full pipeline from natural language input, through SAR representation, to inference output.
AI.conclusion: The architecture makes MIEM and the Track Model immediately deployable with current technology, establishes prior art against proprietary enclosure of the approach, and grounds the method in a theoretical framework linking semantic track representations to neural manifold geometry.

title: Extending Ground-Constraint LiDAR-IMU Calibration to Tilted Surfaces in a Continuous-Time Framework
comment: 8 pages, 13 figures. Submitted to Robotics & Automation Letters
summary: This paper presents a novel method that extends targetless LiDAR-IMU calibration for ground vehicles to non- flat environments. Calibration typically necessitates full exci- tation of the sensor rig, a requirement that is not fulfilled by ground vehicles in normal operation. To address the degenerate planar motion, state-of-the-art methods propose residuals that assume the colinearity of the gravity and physical surface normal vectors, restricting usage to cases where the ground is assumed flat. This paper proposes ground-plane residuals that do not require this assumption, and are applicable for planar motion on a tilted surface. Results are demonstrated on a dataset collected from a Husky ground vehicle, on the M2DGR dataset, as well as on an offroad vehicle dataset. Repeatability is shown to be improved both in tilted and flat-ground scenarios, with strong improvement demonstrated for the tilted case. The implementation and experiments are open-sourced at https://github.com/vkorotkine/licalib_tilted_ground.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a novel targetless LiDAR-IMU calibration method that extends ground vehicle calibration to non-flat environments by proposing ground-plane residuals that do not assume colinearity between gravity and surface normal vectors, enabling accurate calibration under planar motion on tilted surfaces. Results show improved repeatability on flat and especially tilted ground scenarios across multiple datasets.
AI.motivation: Traditional targetless LiDAR-IMU calibration requires full excitation of the sensor rig, which is rarely satisfied by ground vehicles in normal operation. State-of-the-art methods addressing the degenerate planar motion assume colinearity of gravity and surface normal vectors, restricting their applicability to flat ground only. This limits calibration of ground vehicles operating in non-flat, offroad environments.
AI.method: The paper introduces ground-plane residuals that do not require the assumption of gravity and surface normal colinearity. This allows calibration to be performed under planar motion on tilted surfaces. The method is implemented and validated on a Husky ground vehicle dataset, the M2DGR dataset, and an offroad vehicle dataset.
AI.result: The proposed method demonstrates improved repeatability in both tilted and flat-ground scenarios, with particularly strong improvements in the tilted case across all evaluated datasets.
AI.conclusion: The proposed ground-plane residual-based approach successfully extends targetless LiDAR-IMU calibration to non-flat environments, making it applicable to ground vehicles operating on tilted surfaces where prior methods degrade or fail. The implementation and experiments are open-sourced.

title: Same-Player Verification for Account Consistency in Counter-Strike 2
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures, 8 tables. Submitted to IEEE for possible publication
summary: In competitive first-person shooter (FPS) games such as Counter-Strike 2 (CS2), account-integrity review often asks whether an account's recent behavior remains consistent with its historical operator. This consistency question arises in cases such as temporary substitution, rank boosting, and high-skill players using lower-ranked accounts, where manual review requires comparing a current match against multiple historical matches. We formulate this review task as same-player verification: we encode the behavioral trajectory of a single player in a match replay (demo) as a demo-player behavioral fingerprint, and train a model to judge whether two behavioral observations come from the same real player. Grounded in CS2 game understanding, the fingerprints cover crosshair control, movement-stop-fire coordination, economy/buy, combat/engagement, and temporal rhythm. From 1,330 CS2 demos we extract 13,300 demo-player observations, and sample 663,590 same/different pairs from an 88.4M candidate-pair space for supervised training and evaluation. The final pairwise model reaches an average ROC AUC of 0.931 and achieves 0.722 different-player recall at 95% precision. Feature analysis shows that the strongest identity signals come from low-level operations, especially crosshair control, firing rhythm, and movement-stop-fire coordination, indicating that stable low-level mechanical habits are more informative for this verification task than single-match performance outcomes. In the account-history aggregation evaluation, increasing history depth raises AUC from the K=1 single-pair baseline of 0.931 to 0.986 at K=10. These results show that CS2 demo behavior can support supervised same-player verification and account-level identity-consistency modeling through multi-demo history aggregation.

AI.tldr: This paper formulates CS2 account-integrity review as a same-player verification task. The authors extract behavioral fingerprints from match replays (demo recordings) covering crosshair control, movement-stop-fire coordination, economy/buy, combat/engagement, and temporal rhythm. Trained on 13,300 demo-player observations from 1,330 demos with 663,590 sampled pairs, the pairwise model achieves an average ROC AUC of 0.931. Account-history aggregation across K=10 demos raises AUC to 0.986, demonstrating that low-level mechanical habits (crosshair control, firing rhythm, movement-stop-fire coordination) are stronger identity signals than match performance outcomes.
AI.motivation: Account-integrity review in competitive FPS games like CS2 needs automated tools to determine whether an account's recent behavior is consistent with its historical operator. Manual review is time-consuming as it requires comparing current matches against multiple historical ones, especially in cases of temporary substitution, rank boosting, and smurfing (high-skill players using lower-ranked accounts).
AI.method: The authors encode each player's behavioral trajectory in a demo as a demo-player behavioral fingerprint grounded in CS2 game understanding. Fingerprints cover five dimensions: crosshair control, movement-stop-fire coordination, economy/buy decisions, combat/engagement patterns, and temporal rhythm. They construct a supervised pairwise dataset from 1,330 CS2 demos yielding 13,300 demo-player observations, sample 663,590 same/different pairs from an 88.4M candidate-pair space, and train a model to judge whether two behavioral observations come from the same real player. They also evaluate multi-demo history aggregation for account-level consistency.
AI.result: The pairwise same-player verification model achieves an average ROC AUC of 0.931 and 0.722 different-player recall at 95% precision. Feature analysis reveals that low-level mechanical operations—especially crosshair control, firing rhythm, and movement-stop-fire coordination—are the strongest identity signals, outperforming single-match performance outcomes. History aggregation increases AUC from 0.931 (K=1) to 0.986 (K=10).
AI.conclusion: CS2 demo behavior can support supervised same-player verification and account-level identity-consistency modeling. Multi-demo history aggregation substantially improves verification accuracy, confirming that stable low-level mechanical habits are reliable identity indicators for account-integrity review tasks.

title: SkyDrive: Learning to Drive in a New City from Aerial Traffic Monitoring
summary: Autonomous driving has made remarkable progress through imitation learning with massive human demonstration data. However, a trained planner often degrades severely when applied to a new environment zero-shot, because of domain shifts in traffic regulations, road layout and driving behaviors. Therefore, adapting a trajectory planner to a new city typically requires resource-demanding local data collection with a vehicle sensor suite. In this work, we show that driving behavior can be learned from a scalable and efficient alternative. We introduce \emph{SkyDrive}, a framework that utilizes drone-based traffic monitoring to provide efficient supervision for autonomous driving agents in a new environment. While vehicle-based data collection logs the ego and its surroundings, an aerial platform naturally observes many road users simultaneously over an extended field of view. As a result, every vehicle can be a data source with grounded driving behavior, effectively scaling up the amount of supervision. Based on 137 hours of aerial traffic monitoring footage, we extract 650K driving samples and construct a benchmark for trajectory planners and motion predictors. Zero-shot experiments with multiple models reveal significant cross-city domain gaps, but many of them can be alleviated by limited supervision from the sky, e.g., 30 minutes of monitoring per location. Our findings show that aerial traffic monitoring is an efficient and scalable data source for adapting autonomous driving systems in new cities. Data and code will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: SkyDrive is a framework that uses drone-based aerial traffic monitoring to provide scalable and efficient supervision for adapting autonomous driving trajectory planners to new cities, bypassing the need for resource-intensive vehicle-based data collection. Using 137 hours of aerial footage, it extracts 650K driving samples, showing that limited aerial supervision (e.g., 30 minutes per location) significantly alleviates cross-city domain gaps in zero-shot planner performance.
AI.motivation: Autonomous driving planners trained via imitation learning on massive human demonstration data degrade severely when applied zero-shot to new environments due to domain shifts in traffic regulations, road layouts, and driving behaviors. Traditional adaptation requires resource-demanding local vehicle-based data collection, motivating the need for a more scalable and efficient supervision source.
AI.method: SkyDrive leverages drone-based aerial traffic monitoring to observe many road users simultaneously over an extended field of view, treating every vehicle as a grounded data source for driving behavior. The framework constructs a benchmark from 137 hours of aerial footage, extracting 650K driving samples for trajectory planner and motion predictor training and evaluation.
AI.result: Zero-shot experiments with multiple models reveal significant cross-city domain gaps. However, many of these gaps are alleviated with limited aerial supervision, such as just 30 minutes of drone monitoring per location, demonstrating the effectiveness of aerial data for cross-city adaptation.
AI.conclusion: Aerial traffic monitoring serves as an efficient and scalable alternative data source for adapting autonomous driving systems to new cities, significantly reducing the data collection burden compared to traditional vehicle-based approaches.

title: Semantic Graph Unification for Industrial Digital Threads: Bridging 11 Heterogeneous Manufacturing Systems Through Ontology-Driven Knowledge Graphs
summary: Modern manufacturing enterprises operate heterogeneous systems -- ERP, MES, PLM, SCADA, QMS, SCM -- each with its own data model and API. The resulting silos prevent holistic analysis, delay root-cause investigation, and obstruct Industry 4.0 traceability. Point-to-point integration scales as O(n^2) and accumulates brittle dependencies. This paper presents an open framework for semantic graph unification of industrial digital threads. An ontology-driven RDF knowledge graph unifies data from 11 simulated sources across nine domains through a five-stage ETL pipeline with automated entity resolution spanning 97 owl:sameAs identity links. The ontology encompasses 78 RDFS classes, 108 object properties, and 243 data properties, drawing on ISA-95, OPC UA, eClass, the Asset Administration Shell, RAMI 4.0, and additional standards. An automated discovery engine applies nine strategy categories -- cross-station correlation, alarm coverage, ECN impact, CUSUM/EWMA drift detection -- to surface insights spanning system boundaries. The primary empirical result: blocking 24 cross-system tools reduces recall from 1.00 to 0.31 (F1 from 1.00 to 0.48), showing that 69% of discoverable signals require cross-system graph joins. Leave-one-out ablation confirms six of nine strategies contribute unique signals. Verification against a 65-signal manifest (16 positive, 49 null) yields F1 = 1.00 (95% Clopper-Pearson CI [0.79, 1.00]); as the manifest was author-constructed, this constitutes verification not independent validation. The graph is exposed to LLM agents via 287 Model Context Protocol tools as a SPARQL-native semantic layer. Five industry templates (aerospace, CPG, pharma, medical devices, turbine blades) demonstrate schema stability across manufacturing verticals.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an open framework for semantic graph unification of industrial digital threads, using an ontology-driven RDF knowledge graph to integrate 11 heterogeneous manufacturing data sources across nine domains. The framework employs a five-stage ETL pipeline with automated entity resolution (97 owl:sameAs links), an ontology of 78 RDFS classes, 108 object properties, and 243 data properties based on standards like ISA-95, OPC UA, and RAMI 4.0. An automated discovery engine with nine strategy categories surfaces cross-system insights. Empirical results show that 69% of discoverable signals require cross-system graph joins (F1 drops from 1.00 to 0.48 when cross-system tools are blocked), and six of nine strategies contribute unique signals via leave-one-out ablation. The graph is exposed to LLM agents via 287 Model Context Protocol tools as a SPARQL-native semantic layer, with five industry templates demonstrating schema stability.
AI.motivation: Modern manufacturing enterprises operate heterogeneous systems (ERP, MES, PLM, SCADA, QMS, SCM) with disparate data models and APIs, creating data silos that prevent holistic analysis, delay root-cause investigation, and obstruct Industry 4.0 traceability. Point-to-point integration scales as O(n^2) and accumulates brittle dependencies, motivating the need for a unified semantic framework.
AI.method: The framework builds an ontology-driven RDF knowledge graph drawing on ISA-95, OPC UA, eClass, Asset Administration Shell, RAMI 4.0, and other standards. A five-stage ETL pipeline integrates data from 11 simulated sources across nine domains with automated entity resolution generating 97 owl:sameAs identity links. An automated discovery engine applies nine strategy categories (e.g., cross-station correlation, alarm coverage, ECN impact, CUSUM/EWMA drift detection) to surface cross-system insights. The graph is exposed to LLM agents via 287 Model Context Protocol tools as a SPARQL-native semantic layer. Validation includes blocking cross-system tools, leave-one-out ablation, and verification against a 65-signal manifest with Clopper-Pearson confidence intervals.
AI.result: Blocking 24 cross-system tools reduces recall from 1.00 to 0.31 (F1 from 1.00 to 0.48), demonstrating that 69% of discoverable signals require cross-system graph joins. Leave-one-out ablation confirms six of nine strategies contribute unique signals. Verification against a 65-signal manifest (16 positive, 49 null) yields F1 = 1.00 with 95% Clopper-Pearson CI [0.79, 1.00], though acknowledged as author-constructed verification. Five industry templates (aerospace, CPG, pharma, medical devices, turbine blades) demonstrate schema stability.
AI.conclusion: The proposed semantic graph unification framework effectively bridges heterogeneous manufacturing data silos, with strong evidence that cross-system graph joins are essential for discovering a majority of actionable signals in industrial settings. The framework demonstrates schema stability across multiple manufacturing verticals and provides a standards-aligned, LLM-agent-exposable semantic layer for Industry 4.0 traceability and analysis. However, the verification results should be interpreted cautiously as they constitute author-constructed verification rather than independent validation.

title: Sequential Object Placement Optimization with Convex Decomposition
summary: Robotic object packing has been a core challenge for robotic deployment in logistics, industry, etc., due to the curse of dimensionality in combinatorial search and the difficulty of dealing with dynamic and contact constraints for irregularly shaped objects. Current heuristic and learning-based methods assume a limited spatial discretization resolution of space, and computation becomes extremely inefficient as discretization accuracy increases. In this work, we eliminate these assumptions by introducing SOPO-CD, a sequential optimization framework that frames object placement as a differentiable nonlinear optimization problem in a decomposed free space. We prove that placing a convex object inside a convex hull is essentially constraining the vertices of the object inside the convex hull. The constraints and their derivatives can be written in closed form and calculated within $200$ns. We implement a custom solver that achieves optimal placement within tightly constrained space in milliseconds; a $100 \times$ speedup compared to a classical grid search method. We generalize our framework to 2D Tangram, 2D Tetris, and 3D Bin Packing, and have demonstrated strong computational performance and packing utility. We also demonstrate solving a real-world Tangram puzzle online using an Allegro Hand and an Xarm.

AI.tldr: SOPO-CD is a differentiable nonlinear optimization framework for robotic object packing that eliminates spatial discretization assumptions, achieving millisecond-level optimal placement with closed-form constraints, 100x speedup over grid search, and demonstrations across 2D/3D packing tasks and real-world Tangram puzzle solving.
AI.motivation: Robotic object packing suffers from the curse of dimensionality in combinatorial search and challenges from dynamic/contact constraints for irregular shapes. Existing heuristic and learning-based methods rely on discretized spatial resolution, making computation extremely inefficient as discretization accuracy increases.
AI.method: SOPO-CD frames object placement as a differentiable nonlinear optimization problem in a decomposed free space. It proves that placing a convex object inside a convex hull can be reduced to constraining the object's vertices inside the hull, with constraints and derivatives expressed in closed form and computed in under 200ns. A custom solver is implemented to find optimal placement within tight constraints in milliseconds.
AI.result: Achieves a 100x speedup compared to classical grid search methods. The framework generalizes to 2D Tangram, 2D Tetris, and 3D Bin Packing with strong computational performance and packing utility. Real-world online Tangram puzzle solving was demonstrated using an Allegro Hand and an Xarm robot.
AI.conclusion: By formulating packing as differentiable nonlinear optimization with closed-form convex hull constraints, the framework bypasses discretization limitations and achieves orders-of-magnitude speedups while remaining practical for real-world robotic manipulation tasks.

title: post-graph-rag: A PostgreSQL-Native Graph RAG Engine
summary:
Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation connects facts that no single passage states, but current implementations pay for that three times: in infrastructure, requiring a vector store, graph database and document store to be kept consistent; in graph quality, because an extraction pipeline that never refuses output fills the graph with edges that assert nothing; and over time, because a graph that only accumulates treats superseded and current facts alike.
  post-graph-rag is an open-source engine addressing all three. Text chunks with embeddings, a canonical entity graph and community summaries live in one PostgreSQL database, with pgvector for search and edge tables for traversal. Extraction-time invariants run before anything is written: vague predicates, pronominal names and bare quantities are rejected; predicates are normalised onto an optional vocabulary; entities resolve to one vertex per canonical name via model-supplied aliases; and denied relations keep the positive predicate under a negation flag. A temporal layer lets relations carry a validity period from the prose, lets a later document supersede an earlier incompatible assertion from document order alone, and answers as-of queries.
  Against LightRAG on three corpora under identical extraction and embedding models, post-graph-rag builds a denser graph everywhere, up to $2.4\times$ the relations per entity, and a more queryable one: distinct edge labels run at 0.46 to 0.58 per relation, 0.11 under a controlled vocabulary, against 0.77 to 1.33. It answers comparably with lower query latency, and supports temporal evolution the baseline lacks: 13 and 8 relationships superseded on a novel sequence and a decade of filings, against zero. These are engineering measurements, not a benchmark result.
  Code: https://github.com/crajah/post-graph-rag, https://github.com/crajah/post-graph

AI.tldr: post-graph-rag is an open-source graph-based retrieval-augmented generation engine that uses a single PostgreSQL database (with pgvector and edge tables) to eliminate the infrastructure overhead of separate vector, graph, and document stores. It enforces extraction-time invariants for graph quality (rejecting vague predicates, normalizing predicates, resolving entities via aliases, negation flags) and adds a temporal layer for fact validity and supersession. It outperforms LightRAG in graph density and queryability while maintaining comparable answer quality with lower latency.
AI.motivation: Graph-based RAG connects facts across passages, but current implementations suffer from three compounding costs: (1) maintaining three separate data stores (vector, graph, document) in consistency; (2) poor graph quality from extraction pipelines that never refuse output, creating edges that assert nothing; and (3) no temporal handling—graphs only accumulate, treating superseded and current facts equally.
AI.method: post-graph-rag consolidates all data (text chunks with embeddings, canonical entity graph, community summaries) into one PostgreSQL database using pgvector for search and edge tables for traversal. It enforces extraction-time invariants before writing: rejecting vague predicates, pronominal names, and bare quantities; normalizing predicates onto an optional vocabulary; resolving entities to one vertex per canonical name using model-supplied aliases; and representing denied relations with negation flags. A temporal layer allows relations to carry validity periods from prose, supports supersession of earlier incompatible assertions by later documents from document order alone, and enables as-of queries.
AI.result: Against LightRAG on three corpora under identical extraction and embedding models, post-graph-rag builds denser graphs everywhere (up to 2.4x relations per entity) with more queryable edge labels (0.46-0.58 distinct labels per relation, down to 0.11 with a controlled vocabulary, versus 0.77-1.33 for LightRAG). It answers comparably with lower query latency and supports temporal evolution (13 and 8 relationships superseded on a novel sequence and a decade of filings respectively, versus zero for the baseline).
AI.conclusion: post-graph-rag demonstrates that a unified single-database architecture with extraction-time constraints and temporal awareness can address all three shortcomings of graph-based RAG simultaneously. The author frames these as engineering measurements validating the design choices rather than a formal benchmark, with open-source code provided.

title: Control-Oriented Learning for Dynamic Tracking and Stability Analysis of Soft Pneumatic Actuators
summary: Soft pneumatic actuators offer inherent compliance and safe interaction but remain difficult to model and control because of their highly nonlinear, distributed dynamics. We present a control-oriented data-driven modeling and control framework that decomposes actuator behavior into a nonlinear static equilibrium model and a linear residual dynamics model identified using Extended Dynamic Mode Decomposition with control (EDMDc). This representation enables feedforward compensation, task-space feedback control, and local closed-loop stability analysis through an augmented linear model. Experiments achieve approximately 1 mm root mean square error (RMSE) during low-speed (approximately 10 mm/s) trajectory tracking and below 10 mm RMSE at higher speeds (approximately 100 mm/s). The framework further achieves stable tracking of highly dynamic user-generated references with peak accelerations exceeding 25 m/s^2 while simultaneously performing real-time obstacle avoidance. Finally, the proposed stability analysis is experimentally validated by accurately predicting stable, marginal, and unstable operating regimes. These results demonstrate that structured, control-oriented learning provides an accurate and practical framework for soft actuator control.

AI.tldr: A control-oriented data-driven framework for soft pneumatic actuators that decomposes behavior into a nonlinear static equilibrium model and a linear residual dynamics model via EDMDc, achieving ~1 mm RMSE at low speeds, <10 mm RMSE at high speeds, stable tracking of highly dynamic references with real-time obstacle avoidance, and experimentally validated stability prediction.
AI.motivation: Soft pneumatic actuators are difficult to model and control due to their highly nonlinear, distributed dynamics, yet they offer valuable inherent compliance and safe interaction properties.
AI.method: Decomposes actuator behavior into a nonlinear static equilibrium model plus a linear residual dynamics model identified using Extended Dynamic Mode Decomposition with control (EDMDc). This enables feedforward compensation, task-space feedback control, and local closed-loop stability analysis through an augmented linear model.
AI.result: Achieved ~1 mm RMSE at low speeds (~10 mm/s) and below 10 mm RMSE at high speeds (~100 mm/s). Stable tracking of highly dynamic user-generated references with peak accelerations >25 m/s² while performing real-time obstacle avoidance. Stability analysis accurately predicted stable, marginal, and unstable operating regimes.
AI.conclusion: Structured, control-oriented learning provides an accurate and practical framework for soft actuator control, offering both high tracking performance and validated closed-loop stability guarantees.

title: FrontierChallenge: Evaluating Scientific Workflow Completion
summary: Scientific agents increasingly analyze data, execute code, and produce research artifacts, yet most benchmarks emphasize final answers, isolated programs, or a single domain. We introduce FrontierChallenge, a cross-domain benchmark comprising 300 end-to-end scientific workflows. In this paper, we release and evaluate 97 of these tasks, spanning quantum chemistry, molecular dynamics, materials characterization, analytical chemistry, life science, and electrochemistry/environment. Each task provides fixed inputs and specifies a bundle of required scientific deliverables. We evaluate twelve frontier models with three agent scaffolds. Pass Rate measures the fraction of tasks satisfying the full-completion criterion, while Avg. Score captures partial progress. Each of the best-performing configurations completed only 20 of the 97 released tasks, yielding a Pass Rate of 20.6%. Partial progress translated especially poorly into complete delivery in analytical chemistry and electrochemistry/environment: Avg. Scores reached 87.6 and 94.9, but the highest Pass Rates were only 4% and 0%. Among non-passing Claude Code trajectories, 75.5% still ended with language claiming completion. These findings show that neither high partial scores nor confident claims of completion reliably indicate that a scientific task has been fully delivered, highlighting the need to evaluate end-to-end workflow execution and the completeness of scientific deliverables together.

AI.tldr: FrontierChallenge is a cross-domain benchmark of 300 end-to-end scientific workflows (97 released), evaluating twelve frontier models with three agent scaffolds. The best configurations achieve only a 20.6% Pass Rate, and high partial scores (Avg. Score up to 94.9) do not translate into full task completion, with 75.5% of non-passing Claude Code trajectories falsely claiming completion.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for scientific agents emphasize final answers, isolated programs, or single domains, failing to capture the complexity of real scientific work which involves data analysis, code execution, and production of multiple research artifacts across diverse disciplines.
AI.method: Introduces FrontierChallenge, a benchmark of 300 end-to-end scientific workflows (97 released) spanning six domains: quantum chemistry, molecular dynamics, materials characterization, analytical chemistry, life science, and electrochemistry/environment. Each task provides fixed inputs and requires a bundle of scientific deliverables. Twelve frontier models are evaluated using three agent scaffolds, with Pass Rate (full completion) and Avg. Score (partial progress) as metrics.
AI.result: Best configurations completed only 20 of 97 tasks (20.6% Pass Rate). Analytical chemistry and electrochemistry/environment showed high Avg. Scores (87.6 and 94.9) but very low Pass Rates (4% and 0%). Among non-passing Claude Code trajectories, 75.5% ended with language claiming completion despite incomplete delivery.
AI.conclusion: High partial progress scores and confident completion claims do not reliably indicate that scientific tasks have been fully delivered. This highlights the need for evaluation methods that jointly assess end-to-end workflow execution and the completeness of scientific deliverables.

title: CRESSim-Neo: A Batched GPU Simulation Engine for Surgical Robotics and Robot Learning
summary: We introduce CRESSim-Neo, a batched GPU simulation engine for surgical robotics and robot learning. CRESSim-Neo combines position-based simulation of rigid bodies, deformable tissues, fluids, and strands with batched rendering, surgery-specific sensing, and a GPU-resident data pipeline. The engine supports applications including tissue manipulation, fluid suction, suturing, cable-driven robots, and ultrasound image synthesis. Direct access to physics and rendering buffers enables GPU-resident robot learning and zero-copy PyTorch integration using DLPack. We demonstrate CRESSim-Neo across rigid-body, deformable-body, and fluid simulation tasks, including vision-based and surgical robot-learning scenarios. On an NVIDIA RTX 4090, the engine achieves up to 2.03 million environment steps per second for 8192 parallel CartPole environments, and scales to batched surgical scenarios involving tissue deformation, fluid interaction, and ultrasound sensing. Overall, CRESSim-Neo provides a unified and scalable platform for surgical simulation, synthetic data generation, and surgical robot learning.

AI.tldr: CRESSim-Neo is a batched GPU simulation engine for surgical robotics and robot learning, combining position-based simulation of rigid bodies, deformable tissues, fluids, and strands with batched rendering, surgery-specific sensing, and a GPU-resident data pipeline. It supports tissue manipulation, fluid suction, suturing, cable-driven robots, and ultrasound synthesis, with zero-copy PyTorch integration via DLPack. On an RTX 4090 it achieves up to 2.03M environment steps/second for 8192 parallel CartPole environments and scales to batched surgical scenarios.
AI.motivation: To provide a unified, scalable GPU-native simulation platform that addresses the need for high-throughput, realistic surgical simulation and synthetic data generation for surgical robot learning, overcoming limitations of existing simulators that lack batched parallelism, surgery-specific sensing, and tight integration with GPU-resident learning pipelines.
AI.method: The engine combines position-based dynamics for multiple material types (rigid bodies, deformable tissues, fluids, strands) with batched rendering and surgery-specific sensing (e.g., ultrasound synthesis). It provides direct access to physics and rendering buffers, enabling GPU-resident robot learning and zero-copy PyTorch integration via DLPack. All simulation, rendering, and data pipeline components reside on the GPU to avoid CPU-GPU transfer bottlenecks.
AI.result: On an NVIDIA RTX 4090, CRESSim-Neo achieves up to 2.03 million environment steps per second for 8192 parallel CartPole environments. It scales to batched surgical scenarios involving tissue deformation, fluid interaction, and ultrasound sensing, demonstrated across rigid-body, deformable-body, and fluid simulation tasks including vision-based and surgical robot-learning scenarios.
AI.conclusion: CRESSim-Neo provides a unified and scalable platform for surgical simulation, synthetic data generation, and surgical robot learning, bridging the gap between high-fidelity surgical simulation and GPU-resident parallel robot learning.

title: Solving Robust POMDPs with Omega-regular Objectives via Partially Observable Stochastic Games
summary: Robust POMDPs (RPOMDPs) generalize classical POMDPs to the setting where exact transition probabilities are not known -- rather, they are only known to belong to some uncertainty set of values. In this work, we study the problem of solving RPOMDPs with general omega-regular objectives, which subsume a broad class of objectives such as reachability, safety, and linear temporal logic (LTL) objectives. We show that, for (s,a)-rectangular RPOMDPs with polytopic uncertainty sets, the problem of solving RPOMDPs under omega-regular objectives can be reduced to solving partially observable stochastic games (POSGs) under omega-regular objectives. Moreover, we show for the first time that reductions can be constructed in both directions, establishing the semantic equivalence between (s,a)-rectangular RPOMDPs with polytopic uncertainty sets and POSGs. This allows us to derive a range of new computational complexity results, including both upper and lower complexity bounds, on solving RPOMDPs with different omega-regular objectives. As a corollary, we also derive new computational complexity results for RMDPs.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes a bidirectional semantic equivalence between (s,a)-rectangular Robust POMDPs (RPOMDPs) with polytopic uncertainty sets and Partially Observable Stochastic Games (POSGs) under general omega-regular objectives, thereby deriving new computational complexity bounds (both upper and lower) for solving RPOMDPs, with corollary results for RMDPs.
AI.motivation: Robust POMDPs generalize classical POMDPs to settings where transition probabilities are only known to lie within uncertainty sets. While reachability, safety, and LTL objectives are broadly applicable, solving RPOMDPs under general omega-regular objectives remains an open and important problem, particularly regarding their computational complexity and relationship to other formal models.
AI.method: The authors prove that solving (s,a)-rectangular RPOMDPs with polytopic uncertainty sets under omega-regular objectives reduces to solving partially observable stochastic games (POSGs) under omega-regular objectives. Crucially, they demonstrate that reductions can be constructed in both directions, establishing a semantic equivalence between the two frameworks.
AI.result: The bidirectional reductions establish semantic equivalence between (s,a)-rectangular RPOMDPs with polytopic uncertainty sets and POSGs. This yields a range of new computational complexity results, including both upper and lower bounds, for solving RPOMDPs under various omega-regular objectives, as well as new complexity results for RMDPs as corollaries.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides the first systematic complexity characterization of solving RPOMDPs under general omega-regular objectives by leveraging a newly established equivalence with POSGs. This contributes both theoretical insight into the relationship between robust planning and game-theoretic models, and practical guidance on the inherent difficulty of these problems.

title: Longitudinal Robot Learning from Demonstration with Care Providers in a Home Environment
comment: ICRA 2026 Workshop on Bridging the Gap between Robot Learning and Human-Robot Interaction
summary: Learning from demonstration (LfD) methods enable non-expert end users to teach robots novel skills without explicit programming. However most evaluations of the usability of LfD with non-experts has been conducted in controlled laboratory environments with a robotics experimenter present. In this work we identify non-expert end users' key barriers when teaching robots via demonstration without live robotics expert feedback in a home environment. In our human subjects experiment we support the non-expert end users through two forms of demonstrator guidance developed in prior work: pre-training and adaptive feedback. Towards the ecological validity of the evaluation, we conduct this experimentation over multiple visits, with a population of care providers. Finally, we propose to open source the resulting LfD dataset of care providers teaching a robot assistive tasks over multiple visits to a home environment.

AI.tldr: This work evaluates learning from demonstration (LfD) usability with non-expert care providers in home environments over multiple visits, identifying key barriers when no live robotics expert is present. The study supports non-experts via pre-training and adaptive feedback, and proposes releasing the resulting LfD dataset as open source.
AI.motivation: Most LfD usability evaluations with non-experts have been conducted in controlled lab settings with a robotics expert present. This leaves a gap in understanding how non-expert end users fare when teaching robots in real home environments without live expert assistance, which is critical for real-world deployment.
AI.method: Human subjects experiment conducted over multiple visits with care providers as the participant population. Non-expert end users were supported through two forms of demonstrator guidance from prior work: pre-training and adaptive feedback. The evaluation was designed for ecological validity by situating it in home environments.
AI.result: The paper identifies key barriers faced by non-expert end users when teaching robots via demonstration without live robotics expert feedback in home settings. It also produces an LfD dataset of care providers teaching robot assistive tasks across multiple home visits, which the authors propose to open source.
AI.conclusion: The study addresses the ecological validity gap in LfD usability research by moving evaluation out of the lab and into home environments with care providers over multiple visits, and contributes both findings on user barriers and an open-source dataset to support further research.

title: CVE-SAI: Counterfactual Visual Evidence-Guided Selective Attribute Indexing for Risk-Controlled E-commerce Search
summary: Multimodal product models can complete missing e-commerce attributes, yet current methods still optimize attribute-answer accuracy without verifying visual support, conflate transient prediction with persistent index admission, and lack explicit risk control over factually incorrect or visually unsupported values. We address these gaps with Counterfactual Visual Evidence-Guided Selective Attribute Indexing (CVE-SAI), which first infers and freezes an ontology-constrained candidate from the primary image and attribute question without catalog text, and then decides whether that candidate should enter the index. Focus-Zone Distortion (FZD) constructs an attribute-specific visual-dependence proxy through a controlled counterfactual intervention, and Evidence-Guided Attention Redistribution (EGAR) uses the proxy to refine ontology-constrained scoring. The canonical candidate is frozen before evidence necessity, evidence retention, nuisance-transformation stability, and candidate-specific catalog-text conflict audits; catalog text can only tighten admission and cannot revise the candidate. Independent family-level calibration selects one policy with a simultaneous one-sided finite-sample bound under a 5% unsafe-admission budget. Experiments on five visual attributes derived from Amazon Berkeley Objects show that CVE-SAI improves attribute inference and evidence localization, achieves the highest certified admission coverage under the shared risk protocol, and yields the strongest controlled retrieval performance with the lowest unsafe auto-induced exposure among automatic-admission systems. Separating inference from admission therefore enables visually supported attribute completion to improve retrieval while limiting persistent index contamination.

AI.tldr: CVE-SAI is a multimodal product attribute indexing framework that separates attribute inference from index admission, using counterfactual visual evidence to gate which candidates enter the index while enforcing a finite-sample risk bound on unsafe admissions.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal attribute-completion methods optimize only answer accuracy, failing to verify visual support for predictions, conflating transient inference with persistent index admission, and lacking explicit control over factually incorrect or visually unsupported values that contaminate the index.
AI.method: CVE-SAI first infers and freezes an ontology-constrained candidate from the primary image and attribute question (without catalog text), then decides admission. Focus-Zone Distortion (FZD) builds an attribute-specific visual-dependence proxy via controlled counterfactual intervention; Evidence-Guided Attention Redistribution (EGAR) uses the proxy to refine ontology-constrained scoring. The candidate is frozen before audits of evidence necessity, evidence retention, nuisance-transformation stability, and catalog-text conflict; catalog text can only tighten (not revise) admission. Independent family-level calibration selects one policy via a simultaneous one-sided finite-sample bound under a 5% unsafe-admission budget.
AI.result: On five visual attributes from Amazon Berkeley Objects, CVE-SAI improves attribute inference and evidence localization, achieves the highest certified admission coverage under the shared risk protocol, and yields the strongest controlled retrieval performance with the lowest unsafe auto-induced exposure among automatic-admission systems.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling inference from admission enables visually supported attribute completion to enhance retrieval while limiting persistent index contamination, providing a principled risk-aware pathway for multimodal product indexing.

title: Development of a Voice-Controlled Tendon-Driven Bionic Hand
comment: 20 pages, 11 figures, 6 tables. Open-access preprint intended for journal or conference submission
summary: The impairment of the hands can seriously affect the abilities of every individual to perform the every-day activity, so the design of stable and controllable support devices is a significant field of study. This paper is about the design and implementation of an automated bionic hand which is dedicated to the coordinated finger movement through the simplified and efficient actuation mechanism. The method that the proposed system was designed on is the tendon-based method whereby the servo motors generate the movement of the fingers, with assistance of the angular control which is calibrated. An actuation is controlled by a microcontroller that will be programmed by use of an Arduino-based microcontroller to carry out programmed gestures that include open hand, fist, pinch and half flexion. It has an interface that is voice command enabled to make it easy to interact with a Bluetooth based sender receiver architecture which offers an option of executing trained commands which are immediately converted to finger actions. To explore the motions behavior, finger coordination and control response to the input, the behavior of the experiment system is tested. The actuation of the fingers was found to take a total of about 7-8 seconds to achieve full flexion of all fingers in a sequence. The system showed repetitive and constant motion throughout several actuation cycles without loss of any apparent tension or precision of control. There was a stable grasp of objects of different shapes and sizes, which implied consistent coordination between the fingers. These findings indicate that the proposed system offers predictable and steady control behavior and has a simple and efficient mechanical and control architecture.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the design and implementation of an automated bionic hand using a tendon-based actuation mechanism with servo motors and Arduino-based microcontrollers, featuring voice-command control via Bluetooth. The system executes programmed gestures (open hand, fist, pinch, half flexion) and demonstrated full finger flexion in 7-8 seconds with stable object grasping across various shapes and sizes, indicating predictable, steady control and an efficient mechanical architecture.
AI.motivation: Hand impairment significantly limits daily living activities, making the development of stable and controllable assistive devices an important research area. The goal is to create a simple yet efficient bionic hand with coordinated finger movement.
AI.method: The system uses a tendon-based actuation method where servo motors drive finger movement with calibrated angular control. An Arduino-based microcontroller programs gestures such as open hand, fist, pinch, and half flexion. A voice-command interface via Bluetooth sender-receiver architecture converts trained commands into finger actions.
AI.result: Full finger flexion was achieved in approximately 7-8 seconds. The system showed repetitive and constant motion across multiple actuation cycles without loss of tension or control precision. Stable grasping of objects of different shapes and sizes was demonstrated, indicating consistent finger coordination.
AI.conclusion: The proposed bionic hand offers predictable and steady control behavior with a simple, efficient mechanical and control architecture, making it a viable solution for hand-assistive applications.

title: Retrieve, Match, Escalate: Accurate and Scalable Product Linking with VLM-Distilled Cross-Encoders and Agentic VLMs
summary: Product linking, the entity-resolution task of mapping merchant product records to canonical catalog products, consolidates fragmented listings so downstream search, recommendation, and advertising see one clean entry per product. At marketplace scale, billions of noisy, multi-category records must be resolved against tens of millions of canonical products, where scoring every candidate with a single model is either too weak for the hard cases or too costly for the easy ones. We present a production retrieve-then-match cascade that spends computation in proportion to difficulty: retrieval surfaces plausible matches, a lightweight text cross-encoder auto-resolves the high-confidence majority, and an agentic multimodal vision-language model settles the ambiguous remainder by inspecting product images and issuing web searches for evidence that is in neither record. The cross-encoder is distilled from millions of dual-VLM-consensus labels, retiring human annotation from the training set, and is calibrated to auto-accept links at a 98% precision bar validated against a smaller operator-certified audit. The agent is a self-hosted open-weight model that reaches a closed frontier VLM's precision at a four-point recall cost (88% versus 92%) for roughly one-seventh the per-pair cost, with no fine-tuning. Per-pair cost spans nearly five orders of magnitude from the cheap cross-encoder to the frontier VLM, so escalating only the hard tail to the agent raises end-to-end link coverage from the cheap stage's 68% to 77%.

AI.tldr: A production retrieve-then-match cascade for product linking that allocates compute by difficulty: retrieval surfaces candidates, a distilled text cross-encoder auto-resolves the majority at 98% precision, and an agentic multimodal VLM settles the ambiguous tail via image inspection and web search, raising end-to-end link coverage from 68% to 77%.
AI.motivation: At marketplace scale, billions of noisy multi-category records must be matched against tens of millions of canonical products. A single model is either too weak for hard cases or too costly for easy ones, necessitating a difficulty-aware computation allocation strategy.
AI.method: A three-stage cascade: (1) retrieval to surface plausible matches; (2) a lightweight text cross-encoder distilled from millions of dual-VLM-consensus labels (retiring human annotation), calibrated to auto-accept at 98% precision against an operator-certified audit; (3) an agentic self-hosted open-weight multimodal VLM that inspects product images and issues web searches to resolve ambiguous cases, without fine-tuning.
AI.result: The agentic model matches a closed frontier VLM's precision at a four-point recall cost (88% vs 92%) for roughly one-seventh the per-pair cost. Per-pair cost spans nearly five orders of magnitude across the cascade, and escalating only the hard tail to the agent raises end-to-end link coverage from 68% to 77%.
AI.conclusion: A difficulty-scaled retrieve-then-match cascade is an effective production strategy for product linking, achieving high precision at low cost by concentrating expensive reasoning on the ambiguous tail, while eliminating human annotation via VLM-consensus distillation.

title: Generative Action-Chunk Sampling for Adaptive Stiffness Control in Physical Human-Robot Collaboration
summary: Physical human-robot collaboration requires a robot to provide assistance when human intention is clear while remaining compliant when several future motions are plausible. We present an adaptive stiffness framework based on generative action-chunk sampling. Conditioned on an RGB image and external joint-torque estimates, the policy samples multiple future action chunks from an observation-conditioned prior. Variation among the sampled action chunks is used to continuously adapt joint stiffness and damping. Greater variation makes the robot more compliant to facilitate human guidance, whereas lower variation provides firmer assistance. In a real-world collaborative transport task with four possible directions, the proposed method achieved an average success rate of 0.95, compared with 0.83 for a fixed-stiffness ablation and 0.69 for a deterministic baseline. Near direction determination, variation among the sampled action chunks increased and the controller accordingly reduced stiffness. These results suggest that variation among actions sampled by a generative policy can serve as an online control signal for balancing assistance and compliance in physical human-robot interaction.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an adaptive stiffness framework for physical human-robot collaboration that uses a generative policy to sample multiple future action chunks conditioned on RGB images and external joint-torque estimates. The variation among sampled actions continuously adapts joint stiffness and damping: higher variation increases compliance, lower variation provides firmer assistance. In a collaborative transport task with four possible directions, the method achieved 0.95 average success rate versus 0.83 (fixed-stiffness) and 0.69 (deterministic baseline).
AI.motivation: Physical human-robot collaboration requires a robot to provide firm assistance when human intent is clear, but remain compliant when multiple future motions are plausible—a trade-off that fixed-stiffness or deterministic approaches handle poorly.
AI.method: An adaptive stiffness framework based on generative action-chunk sampling. A policy samples multiple future action chunks from an observation-conditioned prior using RGB images and external joint-torque estimates. The variation among sampled action chunks continuously controls joint stiffness and damping.
AI.result: In a real-world collaborative transport task with four possible directions, the method achieved 0.95 average success rate versus 0.83 for a fixed-stiffness ablation and 0.69 for a deterministic baseline.
