Near direction determination, action-chunk variation increased and the controller reduced stiffness accordingly.
AI.conclusion: Variation among actions sampled by a generative policy can serve as an online control signal for balancing assistance and compliance in physical human-robot interaction.

title: LifePlanner: Evaluating LLM Agents for Geo-spatial Planning with Social Media Data
summary: Geo-spatial planning, like trip design, is a realistic testbed for LLM agents because it requires grounded tool use, noisy evidence retrieval, and multi-constraint reasoning. Most benchmarks, however, only provide clean geospatial data and tools, missing the open-ended social signals that people use in daily planning. We introduce LifePlanner, a benchmark that enriches map data with large-scale local social media posts and provides access through an MCP toolset. LifePlanner provides an evaluation suite spanning four task categories and three difficulty levels. Experiments show frontier LLMs perform well on simple retrieval but degrade sharply on complex planning, with the Pass Rate dropping to 40.2%. Results show that failures mainly stem from incomplete evidence acquisition from such a large multimodal database, imprecise tool use, and weak constraint integration rather than model size or reasoning length, suggesting that future progress requires effective grounded planning instead of scaling alone.

AI.tldr: LifePlanner is a benchmark that enriches geospatial map data with large-scale local social media posts and provides an MCP toolset, evaluating LLM agents across four task categories and three difficulty levels for geo-spatial planning. Frontier LLMs achieve 40.2% Pass Rate on complex planning, with failures stemming from incomplete evidence acquisition, imprecise tool use, and weak constraint integration rather than model size or reasoning length.
AI.motivation: Geo-spatial planning is a realistic testbed for LLM agents requiring grounded tool use, noisy evidence retrieval, and multi-constraint reasoning, but existing benchmarks only provide clean geospatial data and tools, missing the open-ended social signals humans use in daily planning.
AI.method: LifePlanner enriches map data with large-scale local social media posts and exposes it through an MCP (Model Context Protocol) toolset, with an evaluation suite spanning four task categories and three difficulty levels.
AI.result: Frontier LLMs perform well on simple retrieval but degrade sharply on complex planning, with Pass Rate dropping to 40.2%. Failures mainly stem from incomplete evidence acquisition from the large multimodal database, imprecise tool use, and weak constraint integration, rather than model size or reasoning length.
AI.conclusion: Future progress in geo-spatial planning for LLM agents requires effective grounded planning rather than scaling alone.

title: RAEM: Robust Autonomous Exploration for Multi-Floor Environments with a Quadruped Robot
summary: In this paper, we propose RAEM, a robust autonomous exploration framework for quadruped robots operating in multi-floor environments. Most existing ground-robot exploration approaches rely on planar traversability representations, which cannot adequately represent the overlapping structures and cross-floor connectivity of multi-floor buildings. Although tomography-based representations provide effective traversability modeling for multi-floor navigation, maintaining a global tomography map incurs substantial computational overhead for online exploration with frequent replanning. Moreover, sparse and fragmented LiDAR observations in stairwells can degrade local traversability estimation, leading to irregular viewpoint placement and temporary topological disconnections. To address these challenges, RAEM adopts a hybrid local-global traversability representation, in which a local tomography map and an explicitly categorized local 3D grid map are used for online terrain analysis and connectivity evaluation, while an elevation-aware global topological graph is incrementally constructed from these local spatial representations for efficient cross-floor exploration planning. We further introduce a staircase center alignment strategy to reduce abrupt yaw variations during climbing and a dual path searching mechanism to recover guidance paths when the global topology is locally disconnected. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate robust and computationally stable autonomous exploration across multi-floor structures, including continuous exploration of a five-floor stairwell.

AI.tldr: RAEM is a robust autonomous exploration framework for quadruped robots in multi-floor environments, using a hybrid local-global traversability representation with tomography maps and elevation-aware global topological graphs, plus a staircase center alignment strategy and dual path searching mechanism for stable cross-floor exploration.
AI.motivation: Existing ground-robot exploration approaches rely on planar traversability representations that cannot adequately handle overlapping structures and cross-floor connectivity in multi-floor buildings. While tomography-based representations model multi-floor traversability well, maintaining a global tomography map is computationally expensive for online exploration with frequent replanning. Additionally, sparse LiDAR observations in stairwells degrade local traversability estimation, causing irregular viewpoint placement and temporary topological disconnections.
AI.method: RAEM uses a hybrid local-global traversability representation: a local tomography map and an explicitly categorized local 3D grid map for online terrain analysis and connectivity evaluation, while an elevation-aware global topological graph is incrementally built from these local spatial representations to enable efficient cross-floor exploration planning. It also introduces a staircase center alignment strategy to reduce abrupt yaw variations during climbing and a dual path searching mechanism to recover guidance paths when global topology is locally disconnected.
AI.result: Extensive simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate robust and computationally stable autonomous exploration across multi-floor structures, including continuous exploration of a five-floor stairwell.
AI.conclusion: The proposed RAEM framework effectively addresses multi-floor exploration challenges for quadruped robots, achieving stable and efficient exploration performance through its hybrid local-global representation and associated planning strategies, validated across both simulation and real-world multi-floor scenarios.

title: SimVerity: When Does Simulated Agent Success Survive Physical Deployment?
comment: Submitted to the Main Technical Track of AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-27); currently under review
summary: Simulated evaluation is widely used to benchmark AI agents, yet how much evidence a simulated pass provides about physical deployment has not been systematically quantified. We present SimVerity, a verdict-transfer assurance framework: it replays matched scenarios on target smart home deployments and cross-validates agent execution against independently qualified physical witnesses. Our evaluation highlights that deployment success is a real-world process, not a static property in simulation: completion, reported state, observable effect, and settled outcome diverged within the same execution. Although an advanced simulator cleared all 240 light trials, a camera caught 42 sub-second failures invisible to settled-state checks. False clearance was predictable: a risk profile learned from measured trials and locked before evaluation predicted failures on a path it never physically measured, beating a property-blind baseline in all eleven held-out sessions across two cohorts. Agent auditability was also measurable: switching one agent loop's model-client/serving configuration raised its scenario-matching share from 52-88% to 100%. Finally, a second qualified simulator added no independent cross-check: it never disagreed on any overlapping case, and only physical measurement exposed their shared blind spots. SimVerity turns verdict transfer into an explicit decision: clear, abstain, or escalate before deployment.

AI.tldr: SimVerity is a verdict-transfer assurance framework that quantifies how well simulated evaluation evidence predicts physical deployment success for AI agents in smart home environments, using matched scenario replay and independent physical witness cross-validation.
AI.motivation: Simulated evaluation is widely used to benchmark AI agents, but the extent to which a simulated pass provides evidence about actual physical deployment success has not been systematically quantified. This gap undermines confidence in simulation-based evaluation as a proxy for real-world performance.
AI.method: SimVerity replays matched scenarios on target smart home deployments and cross-validates agent execution against independently qualified physical witnesses. It measures multiple outcome dimensions (completion, reported state, observable effect, settled outcome), learns a risk profile from measured trials, and formalizes verdict transfer as an explicit decision: clear, abstain, or escalate.
AI.result: The advanced simulator cleared all 240 light trials, but a camera exposed 42 sub-second failures invisible to settled-state checks. A risk profile learned before evaluation predicted failures on unseen paths in all eleven held-out sessions across two cohorts, beating a property-blind baseline. Switching one agent loop's model-client/serving configuration raised scenario-matching share from 52-88% to 100%. A second qualified simulator never disagreed on overlapping cases, offering no independent cross-check.
AI.conclusion: Deployment success is a real-world process, not a static property in simulation. Simulators can share blind spots that only physical measurement reveals, and SimVerity provides a principled framework for deciding whether to clear, abstain, or escalate before deployment based on measured evidence.

title: A Taxonomy of Construction Task Activities for Robot Workers
summary: Recent vision-language-action models offer a path toward robots with broader repertoires than conventional task-specific systems. Construction deployment, however, requires a precise inventory of worker activities and the capabilities needed to execute them. We present TARCAT, an occupation-grounded taxonomy derived from 91 O*NET tasks across seven high-employment construction occupations and 30 instructional videos of physical work. TARCAT defines 41 action primitives in 12 groups and three classes and provides a mechanism for composing parameterized primitive sequences into reusable skills. This human-interpretable structure can organize demonstrations, specify robot requirements, and support coding agents that retrieve and extend skill libraries. We also demonstrate selected primitives on a DOBOT CR3 arm with a CRAFT hand. TARCAT thereby provides a common vocabulary for analyzing human work and developing general-purpose construction robots. Annotations are available at https://github.com/AICPS/TARCAT-Taxonomy.

AI.tldr: TARCAT is an occupation-grounded action taxonomy for construction robotics, derived from 91 O*NET tasks across seven occupations and 30 instructional videos, defining 41 action primitives in 12 groups and 3 classes. It enables composing parameterized primitive sequences into reusable skills, demonstrated on a DOBOT CR3 arm with a CRAFT hand.
AI.motivation: Vision-language-action models promise broader robot repertoires, but construction deployment requires a precise inventory of worker activities and the capabilities needed to execute them. Current systems lack a structured, occupation-grounded vocabulary for analyzing human work and guiding general-purpose construction robot development.
AI.method: The authors construct TARCAT by deriving a taxonomy from 91 O*NET tasks across seven high-employment construction occupations and 30 instructional videos of physical work. The taxonomy defines 41 action primitives organized into 12 groups and three classes, providing a mechanism to compose parameterized primitive sequences into reusable skills.
AI.result: TARCAT provides 41 action primitives in 12 groups and three classes, a human-interpretable structure capable of organizing demonstrations, specifying robot requirements, and supporting coding agents that retrieve and extend skill libraries. Selected primitives were demonstrated on a DOBOT CR3 arm with a CRAFT hand. Annotations are publicly available.
AI.conclusion: TARCAT offers a common vocabulary for analyzing human work and developing general-purpose construction robots, bridging the gap between occupation data and actionable robot capabilities.

title: Auto-Policy, not Auto-Skill: Compiled Agent Skills for the Physical World
comment: Presented at the 1st Workshop on Agent Skills (Agent Skills '26), ACM CAIS 2026, San Jose, May 26, 2026
summary: Self-evolving Skill harnesses (AutoSkills, Hermes Agent) generate more advisory orchestration automatically; their reported gains are efficiency, not safety. This misses the actual gap: a Skill describes how an agent should behave; a Policy decides which behavior is allowed to become an action. Today's format covers the first with markdown and scripts; the second is left to the model. Generating more Skills scales the gap, not the safety, especially when a wrong invocation can unlock a door or move money. Two adjacent attacks are documented: malicious skills compromising cloud software, and jailbroken LLM-controlled robots causing physical harm. Their intersection, malicious agent skills causing physical harm, follows directly but has not been reported. We name this class Borrowed Authority: Skills format gives the receiving agent no typed way to reject an inter-agent permission claim, so a malicious or misused Skill can drive actuation by attaching one. We propose Edge Skillguard, a typed authority layer that lives inside the Skill artifact rather than between tools as workflow engines do, with guards over world state and sensor evidence. On a live edge control-plane testbed, the guards reject 60/60 borrowed-authority requests across five attack variants without blocking benign requests, and the result holds at 5x scale and across hosts over a Tailscale mesh. These results suggest that high-risk Skills should co-package typed invocation policy with procedural knowledge, so that physical actions depend on machine-checkable evidence rather than peer-agent claims.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a security gap in self-evolving skill harnesses: they generate more skills but fail to address the safety gap between describing how an agent should behave (Skills) and deciding which behavior is allowed (Policy). The authors name this class "Borrowed Authority" — where a malicious or misused Skill can drive physical actuation by attaching an inter-agent permission claim. They propose Edge Skillguard, a typed authority layer embedded within the Skill artifact with guards over world state and sensor evidence, which rejected 60/60 borrowed-authority requests across five attack variants on a live edge control-plane testbed without blocking benign requests, holding at 5x scale and across a Tailscale mesh.
AI.motivation: Existing self-evolving skill harnesses (AutoSkills, Hermes Agent) report efficiency gains but not safety improvements. This misses the actual gap: Skills describe behavior but Policy (which behaviors are allowed) is left to the model, so generating more Skills scales the gap rather than safety. Two adjacent attacks (malicious skills compromising cloud software, jailbroken LLM-controlled robots causing physical harm) suggest their intersection — malicious agent skills causing physical harm — is a real but unreported threat.
AI.method: The authors define the "Borrowed Authority" attack class: the Skills format gives receiving agents no typed way to reject inter-agent permission claims. They propose Edge Skillguard, a typed authority layer living inside the Skill artifact (not between tools as workflow engines do), with guards over world state and sensor evidence. They evaluate on a live edge control-plane testbed testing five attack variants at 1x and 5x scale, and across hosts over a Tailscale mesh.
AI.result: Edge Skillguard rejected 60/60 borrowed-authority requests across five attack variants without blocking any benign requests. The results held at 5x scale and across hosts over a Tailscale mesh.
AI.conclusion: High-risk Skills should co-package typed invocation policy with procedural knowledge, so that physical actions depend on machine-checkable evidence rather than peer-agent claims. This establishes a new security layer for agent skill execution in physically-embodied or safety-critical contexts.

title: LAC: Linear and Angular Compliance for Humanoid Whole-body Control
summary: Real-world humanoid tasks involve physical interaction with objects and humans, yet current controllers either reject external forces as disturbances or restrict compliance to limited body links while ignoring angular effects. We present LAC, a general whole-body controller that simultaneously realizes commanded Linear and Angular Compliance for wrenches applied to the upper body. First, we synthesize whole-body compliant responses into a large-scale augmented dataset. Sampled force and couple events are imposed on contact frames extracted from human interaction data. At each contact link, the external force and a virtual torque from the passively yielding kinematic chain drive a virtual admittance under the commanded stiffness. Subsequently, teacher-student reinforcement learning trains a single policy to track the compliant motions under external wrenches. Finally, extensive simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate whole-body compliant responses to wrenches across the upper body, monotonic modulation over the full range of both stiffness commands, and applicability to teleoperated loco-manipulation tasks. Project website: https://lac-humanoid.github.io/

AI.tldr: LAC is a whole-body controller for humanoid robots that simultaneously realizes commanded linear and angular compliance for external wrenches applied to the upper body, trained via teacher-student reinforcement learning on an augmented dataset and validated in simulation and real-world experiments including teleoperated loco-manipulation.
AI.motivation: Real-world humanoid tasks involve physical interaction with objects and humans, yet current controllers either reject external forces as disturbances or restrict compliance to limited body links while ignoring angular (torque/couple) effects. There is a need for a general whole-body controller that handles both linear and angular compliance across the entire upper body.
AI.method: The authors synthesize whole-body compliant responses into a large-scale augmented dataset by imposing sampled force and couple events on contact frames extracted from human interaction data. At each contact link, the external force and a virtual torque from the passively yielding kinematic chain drive a virtual admittance under commanded stiffness. Teacher-student reinforcement learning then trains a single policy to track compliant motions under external wrenches.
AI.result: Extensive simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate whole-body compliant responses to wrenches across the upper body, monotonic modulation over the full range of both stiffness commands, and applicability to teleoperated loco-manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: LAC achieves general whole-body linear and angular compliance for humanoid robots under external wrenches applied to the upper body, enabling compliant physical interaction in real-world tasks such as teleoperated loco-manipulation.

title: PhysElite: How Far Are LLMs from Solving Olympiad-Level Physics Problems?
summary: Understanding how (multimodal) large language models perform on physics problems requires benchmarks that reflect the difficulty and breadth of expert-level physical reasoning. Existing physics benchmarks remain limited in the following two important ways: (1) short of high-difficulty datasets, and (2) lack of comprehensive coverage of visual forms, knowledge points, and step-by-step solution processes. As a result, model performance on current datasets may not be fully representative of their ability to solve complex physics problems. To address these issues, we present PhysElite, a large-scale bilingual multimodal benchmark for Olympiad-level physics reasoning. PhysElite contains 11,586 Olympiad-tier problems. For each problem, we provide corresponding visual diagrams, step-by-step bilingual Chinese-English solution derivations, and the final answer. We benchmark 18 open-source and closed-source MLLMs, and find that even the strongest model reaches only 33.7% answer accuracy. We additionally conduct step-level process evaluation to diagnose where models fail in the reasoning chain. Our datasets are released at https://huggingface.co/datasets/physelite/PhysElite.

AI.tldr: PhysElite is a large-scale bilingual (Chinese-English) multimodal benchmark containing 11,586 Olympiad-level physics problems with visual diagrams, step-by-step solution derivations, and final answers. Benchmarking 18 open and closed-source MLLMs shows the strongest model achieves only 33.7% accuracy, along with step-level process evaluation to diagnose reasoning failures.
AI.motivation: Existing physics benchmarks lack high-difficulty problems and comprehensive coverage of visual forms, knowledge points, and step-by-step solutions, making current evaluations unrepresentative of models' ability to solve complex physics problems.
AI.method: Constructs PhysElite, a large-scale bilingual multimodal benchmark with 11,586 Olympiad-tier physics problems, each accompanied by visual diagrams, step-by-step bilingual (Chinese-English) solution derivations, and final answers. Evaluates 18 open-source and closed-source MLLMs on both answer accuracy and step-level process reasoning.
AI.result: The strongest evaluated model achieves only 33.7% answer accuracy on PhysElite. Step-level process evaluation further identifies specific points of failure in models' reasoning chains.
AI.conclusion: Current MLLMs remain far from expert-level physics reasoning, as evidenced by low accuracy on Olympiad-tier problems; PhysElite provides a more comprehensive and difficult benchmark to better measure and diagnose these limitations.

title: SUPER ODOMETRY 2.0: Resilient Odometry via Hierarchical Adaptation
summary: Resilient and robust odometry is crucial for autonomous systems operating in complex and dynamic environments. Existing odometry systems often struggle with severe sensory degradations and extreme conditions such as smoke, sandstorms, snow, or low-light conditions, threatening both the safety and functionality of robots. To address these challenges, we present Super Odometry, a sensor fusion framework that dynamically adapts to varying levels of environmental degradation. Super Odometry employs a hierarchical structure to integrate four core modules from lower-level to higher-level adaptability including adaptive feature selection, adaptive state direction selection, adaptive engine selection, and a novel learning- based inertial odometry. The inertial odometry, trained on over 100 hours of heterogeneous robotic platforms, captures comprehensive motion dynamics. Super Odometry elevates the inertial measurement unit (IMU) to equal importance with camera and LiDAR within the sensor fusion framework, providing a reliable fallback when exteroceptive sensors fail. Super Odometry has been validated across 200 kilometers and 800 operational hours on a fleet of aerial, wheeled, and legged robots, under diverse sensor configurations, environmental degradation, and aggressive motion profiles. It marks an important step towards safe and long-term robotic autonomy in all-degraded environments.

AI.tldr: Super Odometry is a hierarchical sensor fusion framework for robust robot odometry that dynamically adapts to environmental degradation (smoke, sandstorms, snow, low-light) by integrating adaptive feature selection, adaptive state direction selection, adaptive engine selection, and a novel learning-based inertial odometry—elevating the IMU to equal importance with camera and LiDAR. Validated over 200 km and 800 hours across aerial, wheeled, and legged robots.
AI.motivation: Existing odometry systems fail under severe sensory degradation and extreme conditions such as smoke, sandstorms, snow, or low-light, threatening the safety and functionality of autonomous robots. A robust solution that dynamically adapts to varying environmental degradation levels is needed.
AI.method: A hierarchical sensor fusion framework with four core modules of increasing adaptability: (1) adaptive feature selection, (2) adaptive state direction selection, (3) adaptive engine selection, and (4) a novel learning-based inertial odometry trained on >100 hours of heterogeneous robotic platform data. The framework assigns equal importance to IMU, camera, and LiDAR, with the inertial odometry serving as a reliable fallback when exteroceptive sensors fail.
AI.result: Validated across 200 kilometers and 800 operational hours on aerial, wheeled, and legged robots under diverse sensor configurations, environmental degradation conditions, and aggressive motion profiles—demonstrating robust performance in all-degraded environments.
AI.conclusion: Super Odometry marks an important step toward safe, long-term robotic autonomy in all-degraded environments by providing a resilient odometry system that maintains reliability through hierarchical adaptability and IMU-centric fallback.

title: Towards Reliable, Generalizable, and Specific In-Context Knowledge Editing via Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning
comment: Our work proposes a multi-objective reinforcement learning algorithm that optimizes prompt construction for reliable, generalizable, and specific in-context knowledge-editing
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are powerful but limited by static parametric knowledge that becomes outdated once pretraining ends. Knowledge editing addresses this problem by updating model behavior on target facts without full retraining. In particular, in-context knowledge editing has gained attention because it is training-free and readily applicable to black-box LLMs. Recent reinforcement learning (RL)-based approaches improve over fixed retrieval strategies by adapting prompt construction to the quantity-quality trade-off. Despite initial success, they fail to model the prompt as a structured entity under the distinct and often competing objectives of reliability, generality, and specificity. Previous methods largely optimize a single objective and make decisions over only part of the prompt construction process, thereby overlooking both the balance of different objectives and the global organization of demonstrations. We propose Multi-Objective In-context Knowledge Editing (MO-IKE), a multi-objective RL algorithm that formulates prompt construction for in-context knowledge editing as a Constrained Markov Decision Process. MO-IKE trains a dynamic retriever to optimize competing objectives in knowledge editing, enabling more balanced and globally coherent prompt construction. On Llama-3.2, MO-IKE improves edit success (reliability) from 85.0% to 92.0%, paraphrase consistency (generality) from 77% to 79%, while increasing retention rate (specificity) by 23.0% compared to prior RL-based methods.

AI.tldr: MO-IKE is a multi-objective reinforcement learning algorithm for in-context knowledge editing in LLMs that formulates prompt construction as a Constrained Markov Decision Process, jointly optimizing reliability, generality, and specificity to achieve balanced and globally coherent demonstration selection.
AI.motivation: LLMs suffer from outdated parametric knowledge after pretraining. While in-context knowledge editing offers a training-free, black-box-friendly solution, existing RL-based approaches fail to treat prompts as structured entities under multiple, often competing objectives (reliability, generality, specificity). Prior methods optimize a single objective and consider only part of the prompt construction process, missing both objective balance and global demonstration organization.
AI.method: The paper proposes Multi-Objective In-context Knowledge Editing (MO-IKE), which formulates prompt construction for in-context knowledge editing as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP). MO-IKE trains a dynamic retriever as a multi-objective RL agent to optimize competing objectives simultaneously, enabling balanced and globally coherent prompt construction.
AI.result: On Llama-3.2, MO-IKE improves edit success (reliability) from 85.0% to 92.0%, paraphrase consistency (generality) from 77% to 79%, and increases retention rate (specificity) by 23.0% compared to prior RL-based methods.
AI.conclusion: MO-IKE demonstrates that modeling prompt construction as a constrained multi-objective RL problem yields superior, more balanced performance across all three key knowledge editing objectives compared to single-objective RL baselines.

title: Towards safe and optimal flight: Viability Kernel MPC for Fully Actuated Multirotor
summary: Industrial aerial robotics demands safety guarantees for navigation in unstructured environments while optimizing performance and computational efficiency. This paper presents a method for generating safe pose trajectories for fully actuated multirotors within a Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework, leveraging both viability theory and data-driven methods. Obstacle avoidance is enforced through dynamically computed axis-aligned bounding boxes, providing formal safety guarantees without exhaustive offline reachability analysis. Numerical simulations on a fully actuated tilted hexarotor validate the approach, demonstrating successful navigation in cluttered environments with real-time computational performance.

AI.tldr: A method for generating safe pose trajectories for fully actuated multirotors in an MPC framework, combining viability theory and data-driven methods with axis-aligned bounding boxes for formal obstacle avoidance guarantees, validated via simulations on a tilted hexarotor.
AI.motivation: Industrial aerial robotics requires safety guarantees for navigation in unstructured environments while balancing performance and computational efficiency. Traditional reachability-based safety analysis is computationally exhaustive and impractical in real-time settings.
AI.method: The approach integrates viability theory with data-driven methods within a Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework. Obstacle avoidance is enforced via dynamically computed axis-aligned bounding boxes, which provide formal safety guarantees without requiring exhaustive offline reachability analysis.
AI.result: Numerical simulations on a fully actuated tilted hexarotor demonstrate successful navigation in cluttered environments with real-time computational performance, validating the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
AI.conclusion: The method achieves both formal safety guarantees and real-time computational feasibility for fully actuated multirotor navigation, making it suitable for industrial aerial robotics applications in unstructured environments.

title: FuzzingBrain-Bench V1: Evaluating Open-Ended Bug Discovery by LLMs
comment: 21 pages, 12 figures, 7 tables. Ze Sheng and Aleksandar Kezic contributed equally. Benchmark corpus and harnesses: https://github.com/fuzzingbrain/FuzzingBrain-Bench Counts verified against the built PDF and sources: 21 pages, 12 figure environments, 7 tables
summary:
Evaluating the ability of large language models (LLMs) to discover software bugs is increasingly important. Existing benchmarks typically evaluate this capability by asking the model to generate a proof-of-concept input that triggers a predefined target vulnerability. However, this setup may overlook valid crashes discovered by the model when they do not match the predefined target. As a result, the evaluation may not reflect the model's real capability.
  We present FuzzingBrain-Bench, a benchmark for assessing AI models' ability to discover bugs in open-source software. Models are given an open-source project and a sanitizer-instrumented harness in a self-contained Docker image. Their goal is to generate inputs that trigger as many distinct crashes as possible through the harness. A model's performance on each challenge is scored based on the number of distinct crash signatures it produces, capped at a predefined maximum and weighted by a difficulty coefficient.
  FuzzingBrain-Bench V1 consists of 77 challenges drawn from 43 open-source projects, with 36 C, 32 C++, and 9 Java/JVM challenges. We evaluate Claude Haiku 4.5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Claude Opus 4.8 on the full benchmark. Claude Opus 4.8 performs best, triggering crashes in 60 of 77 challenges and achieving a score of 196 out of 579. None of the three models triggers a crash in 13 challenges. The FuzzingBrain-Bench corpus and harnesses are publicly available at https://github.com/fuzzingbrain/FuzzingBrain-Bench.

AI.tldr: This paper presents FuzzingBrain-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs' ability to discover software bugs by generating inputs that trigger distinct crashes through sanitizer-instrumented harnesses in Docker containers, addressing limitations of existing benchmarks that only check for predefined target vulnerabilities.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM bug-discovery benchmarks typically require the model to generate a proof-of-concept input for a predefined target vulnerability, which may overlook valid crashes that don't match the predefined target, thus not accurately reflecting the model's real bug-finding capability.
AI.method: The benchmark gives models an open-source project and a sanitizer-instrumented harness in a self-contained Docker image. Models must generate inputs that trigger as many distinct crashes as possible. Performance is scored by counting distinct crash signatures, capped at a predefined maximum and weighted by a difficulty coefficient.
AI.result: FuzzingBrain-Bench V1 contains 77 challenges from 43 open-source projects (36 C, 32 C++, 9 Java/JVM). Claude Opus 4.8 performed best, triggering crashes in 60 of 77 challenges with a score of 196 out of 579. None of the three models (Claude Haiku 4.5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Opus 4.8) triggered crashes in 13 challenges.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark provides a more holistic evaluation of LLM bug-discovery capabilities by rewarding any distinct crash discovered rather than only matching predefined vulnerabilities, and the corpus and harnesses are publicly released for community use.

title: Transient multimode heat transfer of an industrial automated tape laying process under rapidly changing conditions
summary: This work presents a transient heat-transfer model of an industrial automated tape laying (ATL) process designed to overcome the limitations of conventional thermal models in composite manufacturing. The model solves the heat-conduction equation with coupled advection, conduction, convection, and radiation. A key innovation is the implementation of an analytical view factor approach that accounts for finite emitter and tape widths, thereby correcting systematic overestimations of radiative heat flux inherent in 1.5D simplifications. Furthermore, a local convection assessment incorporates mixed convection effects characterized by the Richardson number, ensuring accuracy across a wide range of process speeds. The ATL system is represented by two interacting subsystems: the moving tape substrate and the infrared heat sources. The tape is discretized using a two-node model that resolves the physical phase shift between the heated and monitored surfaces. Numerical stability under high dynamics is ensured by a monolithic solution strategy using a high-order implicit integration scheme. Model predictions were validated on an industrial ATL line, demonstrating an overall deviation of only 1.08% (NRMSE) under rapid velocity and current modulations. This framework provides a high-fidelity, physics-based foundation for thermal state estimation, supporting consistent in-situ consolidation and improved part quality.

AI.tldr: A transient heat-transfer model for industrial automated tape laying (ATL) that couples advection, conduction, convection, and radiation. It uses an analytical view factor approach to correct radiative flux overestimation, a Richardson-number-based mixed convection model, a two-node tape discretization, and a high-order implicit monolithic solver, validated on an industrial line with only 1.08% NRMSE error.
AI.motivation: Conventional thermal models in composite manufacturing suffer from simplifications (e.g., 1.5D radiative view factors) that systematically overestimate heat flux and lose accuracy across varying process speeds, limiting thermal state estimation fidelity needed for consistent in-situ consolidation and part quality.
AI.method: The model solves the heat-conduction equation with coupled advection, conduction, convection, and radiation. It implements an analytical view factor accounting for finite emitter and tape widths, a local convection model with mixed convection characterized by the Richardson number, a two-node tape discretization resolving the phase shift between heated and monitored surfaces, and a monolithic solution with a high-order implicit integration scheme for numerical stability.
AI.result: Validation on an industrial ATL line under rapid velocity and current modulations showed an overall deviation of only 1.08% (NRMSE).
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a high-fidelity, physics-based foundation for thermal state estimation, supporting consistent in-situ consolidation and improved part quality in automated tape laying.

title: Tunable Tool-Call Rates in LLM Agents via Representation Steering
summary: Deciding whether to call a tool is a core competence of an LLM agent, and a costly one to get wrong: needless calls add latency, accrue cost, and may trigger irreversible side effects, while missing calls leave the model confidently wrong on questions it could only answer through tool-calls. Models manage this balance poorly, both over-using and under-using tools. Existing methods such as post-training and prompt engineering are expensive and difficult to modify at inference time. We show that whether an instruction-tuned model calls a tool can be controlled by a single linear direction in its residual stream, extracted without any training from the model's own tool-use preference signal and turned into an inference-time intervention with no prompt change. Adding the direction with strength $α$ moves the call rate monotonically from near $0\% $ to over $90\%$ while keeping calls well-formed. The steering works in both directions: dialing it down suppresses calls, and dialing it up induces new calls that land precisely on the questions the model cannot answer from its own knowledge. We also show that the direction generalizes to unseen tools with strength comparable to each tool's own direction and without favoring any specific tool choice. With live tool execution, a single sweep of the steering traces a cost/accuracy Pareto frontier and nearly doubles open-domain QA accuracy ($0.29 \! \rightarrow \! 0.56$); the same recipe transfers across a diverse range of models spanning dense, MoE, and multimodal architectures, without any training. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/YuqiChen4188/Steering-Tool-Use-Propensity.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that an LLM's propensity to call tools can be controlled via a single linear direction in its residual stream, extracted without training from the model's own tool-use preference signal. This inference-time intervention (steering) can monotonically push tool call rates from near 0% to over 90% while keeping calls well-formed, and generalizes across unseen tools and multiple model architectures, enabling a cost/accuracy Pareto frontier that nearly doubles open-domain QA accuracy.
AI.motivation: Tool-calling decisions in LLM agents are costly to get wrong—unnecessary calls add latency and cost, while missing calls leave the model confidently wrong. Existing approaches like post-training and prompt engineering are expensive and hard to modify at inference time. The paper seeks a lightweight, training-free, inference-time method to control tool-use propensity.
AI.method: The authors extract a single linear direction from the model's residual stream using the model's own tool-use preference signal, with no training required. This direction is turned into an inference-time intervention by adding it with strength α, which shifts the model's tool-calling probability. The steering works bidirectionally (suppress or induce calls) and is evaluated across dense, MoE, and multimodal models with live tool execution.
AI.result: Adding the steering direction with strength α moves call rates monotonically from near 0% to over 90% while maintaining well-formed tool calls. Dialing down suppresses calls; dialing up induces calls that land precisely on questions the model cannot answer from its own knowledge. The direction generalizes to unseen tools without favoring specific tools. With live tool execution, a sweep of steering traces a cost/accuracy Pareto frontier, nearly doubling open-domain QA accuracy (0.29 → 0.56). The recipe transfers across dense, MoE, and multimodal architectures without training.
AI.conclusion: Steering tool-use propensity via a single residual-stream direction provides a training-free, inference-time mechanism to precisely control when an LLM agent calls tools. This offers a practical alternative to expensive post-training or prompt engineering, yielding significant accuracy gains at controlled cost across diverse model architectures.

title: Dynamic Modeling of a Welding Torch Umbilical and Its Impact on Robot Dynamics
summary: Robotic welding is widely used in industrial manufacturing, where the welding torch is often connected to the generator through an external umbilical. With the increasing deployment of lightweight and collaborative robots, the dynamic influence of this umbilical can significantly affect the robot motion and the actuation forces. This paper proposes a constrained multibody dynamic model of a welding umbilical, represented as a serial chain of rigid bodies interconnected by passive joints with elastic and dissipative effects. Prescribed motions at the distal anchor point are introduced through holonomic kinematic constraints. The equations of motion are reduced by projecting the dynamics onto the subspace of admissible velocities, yielding an efficient formulation free of Lagrange multipliers. The reaction wrench exerted by the umbilical on the robot is explicitly recovered. A planar case study illustrates the approach.

AI.tldr: A constrained multibody dynamics model of a robotic welding umbilical is proposed, represented as a serial chain of rigid bodies with passive elastic-dissipative joints and holonomic constraints at the distal anchor. The model is reduced via projection onto the subspace of admissible velocities, enabling efficient, Lagrange-multiplier-free dynamics and explicit recovery of the reaction wrench on the robot.
AI.motivation: Lightweight and collaborative robots are increasingly used in welding, where the external umbilical connecting the torch to the generator exerts dynamic loads that can significantly influence robot motion and actuation forces. An accurate, efficient model of the umbilical's dynamic behavior is needed.
AI.method: The umbilical is modeled as a serial chain of rigid bodies interconnected by passive joints with elastic and dissipative elements. Prescribed motions at the distal anchor are enforced via holonomic kinematic constraints. The equations of motion are projected onto the subspace of admissible velocities to eliminate Lagrange multipliers, yielding an efficient reduced formulation. The reaction wrench on the robot is then explicitly recovered. A planar case study is presented.
AI.result: The approach yields an efficient, multiplier-free dynamic formulation of the welding umbilical, with explicit recovery of the reaction wrench exerted on the robot. A planar case study demonstrates the method's applicability.
AI.conclusion: The proposed constrained multibody formulation provides an efficient means of modeling the dynamic influence of a welding umbilical on a robot, with the planar case study validating the methodology.

title: Federation Is Nearly Free, Reasoning Is Not: Tradeoffs for AI Co-Scientists in Protein Characterization Workflows
comment: 24 Pages, 4 main figures, 5 main tables, 2 supplementary figures
summary: Natural language driven autonomous co-scientist workflows involve a fundamental trade-off between flexibility and reasoning at the expense of determinism, reproducibility, and observability. Such agents increasingly must communicate across institutional boundaries, where federation topology can shape latency and cost. We systematically evaluated these tradeoffs using a controlled ablation on a production agentic platform for science. We use a verifiable task: given a protein sequence, we ask an agent to confidently characterize its function by routing across common tools. We compare federation topology, classic RL vs LLM-driven harnesses, language model, and prompt expertise. We also stratify results by protein novelty. We find that the choice of LLM dominated prediction quality far more than topology or prompting (Opus ~92%-94% vs o4-mini ~40%-50%). The PPO policy was nearly as accurate as the best LLM (88%) at zero token cost, fastest latency, and perfect consistency, but yields no reasoning trace. Expert prompted LLMs reached the highest accuracy but were high-cost and less consistent; prompt dependence was largest when the task was hardest. Federation imposed a negligible penalty on performance. These results offer actionable guidance for deploying agents for scientific workflows: for routine, verifiable tasks, a cheap deterministic policy delivers near-frontier accuracy with complete reproducibility, while flexible LLM reasoning is best reserved for open-ended discovery.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates trade-offs in natural language driven autonomous co-scientist agent workflows: flexibility vs. reasoning vs. determinism/reproducibility/observability, across federation topologies, training paradigms (classic RL/PPO vs. LLM harnesses), model choice, and prompt expertise. On a verifiable protein function characterization task, LLM choice dominated accuracy (Opus ~92-94% vs o4-mini ~40-50%), PPO policies achieved near-frontier accuracy (88%) at zero token cost with perfect consistency but no reasoning trace, expert prompts reached highest accuracy at high cost, and federation imposed negligible performance penalty.
AI.motivation: To provide actionable guidance on how to deploy autonomous agents for scientific workflows by systematically quantifying the trade-offs between model choice, training paradigm, prompting, and federation topology under controlled conditions, rather than relying on anecdotal or ad hoc evaluations.
AI.method: Controlled ablation study on a production agentic platform for science using a verifiable task: characterize a protein's function by routing across common tools given its sequence. Comparisons include federation topology, classic RL (PPO) vs LLM-driven harnesses, choice of language model, and prompt expertise level. Results are stratified by protein novelty.
AI.result: LLM choice dominated prediction quality (Opus ~92-94% vs o4-mini ~40-50%); PPO policy achieved ~88% accuracy at zero token cost with fastest latency and perfect consistency but no reasoning trace; expert-prompted LLMs reached highest accuracy but at high cost with less consistency; prompt dependence increased with task difficulty; federation imposed negligible performance penalty.
AI.conclusion: For routine, verifiable scientific tasks, a cheap deterministic policy (PPO) delivers near-frontier accuracy with complete reproducibility, while flexible LLM reasoning should be reserved for open-ended discovery where its interpretability and adaptability justify the cost and variability.

title: A Tendon-Driven Five-Fingered Hand with Distributed Tactile Perception for Dexterous Manipulation
comment: Accepted by International Conference on Service Robotics (ICoSR) 2026
summary: To apply the techniques of embodied artificial intelligence to human-oid robots for complex manipulations, dexterous robotic hands are indispensable, which are restricted by the dexterity and tactile perception capability. In this work, we proposed a novel design of tendon-driven five-fingered hand with dis-tributed tactile perception. With a soft-rigid-hybrid structure employed, both compliance and operational force are endowed to the hand. Dual-modality tactile sensing elements are distributed on the distal and middle phalanges of all five fingers, enabling the simultaneous detection of static contact and dynamic force variations. Manipulation experiments, including counting gestures, finger-to-thumb pinching, object grasping, and bottle-grasp tactile recording, demonstrate the feasibility of the integrated actuation-perception system.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a novel tendon-driven five-fingered dexterous robotic hand with a soft-rigid hybrid structure and distributed dual-modality tactile sensing on all phalanges, enabling simultaneous static contact and dynamic force detection for complex manipulations on humanoid robots.
AI.motivation: Embodied AI applied to humanoid robots for complex manipulation requires dexterous robotic hands, but existing hands are limited by their dexterity and tactile perception capabilities.
AI.method: A tendon-driven five-fingered hand with a soft-rigid-hybrid structure is proposed, which provides both compliance and operational force. Dual-modality tactile sensing elements are distributed on the distal and middle phalanges of all five fingers to simultaneously detect static contact and dynamic force variations.
AI.result: Manipulation experiments—including counting gestures, finger-to-thumb pinching, object grasping, and bottle-grasp tactile recording—demonstrated the feasibility of the integrated actuation-perception system.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hand design successfully integrates actuation and distributed tactile perception, making it viable for complex manipulation tasks in embodied AI applications on humanoid robots.

title: LLM-Driven, Datasheet-Aware Automated Hardware Compatibility Verification for Early-Stage, Pre-Schematic Embedded System Design
summary: We present an LLM-driven, datasheet-aware framework for early-stage hardware compatibility verification that identifies documentation-level interface incompatibilities based on hardware datasheets and high-level component connectivity descriptions. It does not require, and can therefore be used, before detailed schematic simulation and implementation. We view trustworthy LLM-assisted design automation not as directly generating answers from documents, but as transforming engineering information through traceable verification stages. Given hardware datasheets and high-level component connectivity descriptions, the framework constructs a design graph that captures device connectivity and shared interaction domains, retrieves only the engineering properties required by explicit, domain-oriented verification criteria , and generates deterministic scripts for compatibility evaluation. By decomposing compatibility analysis into modular stages and preserving intermediate results, the framework reduces context overhead, improves transparency and tractability, enables scaling, and avoids reliance on LLMs for numerical computation. Evaluated on seven embedded-system designs comprising 34 datasheets, our framework achieves 97.5% compatibility-verification accuracy and an 8.6 times reduction in input context size compared with ``upload-and-query'' workflows. These results demonstrate the feasibility of LLM-assisted, specification-based hardware compatibility verification at an early design stage, as well as the need for, and substantial benefits of, modular task decomposition, formalized verification criteria, and task-aware compact context construction.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an LLM-driven, datasheet-aware framework for early-stage hardware compatibility verification that detects documentation-level interface incompatibilities using datasheets and high-level connectivity descriptions, without requiring detailed schematic simulation. The framework builds a design graph, retrieves only engineering properties needed by explicit verification criteria, and generates deterministic scripts for compatibility evaluation, achieving 97.5% accuracy and 8.6× context reduction across 34 datasheets from 7 designs.
AI.motivation: Early-stage hardware compatibility verification is critical but currently requires detailed schematic simulation and implementation. The authors aim to enable verification at the documentation level, before such detailed steps, and to establish trustworthy LLM-assisted design automation by transforming engineering information through traceable verification stages rather than relying on LLMs to directly generate answers from documents.
AI.method: The framework takes hardware datasheets and high-level component connectivity descriptions as input, constructs a design graph capturing device connectivity and shared interaction domains, retrieves only the engineering properties required by explicit, domain-oriented verification criteria, and generates deterministic scripts for compatibility evaluation. The approach decomposes compatibility analysis into modular stages while preserving intermediate results, reducing context overhead and avoiding LLM dependency for numerical computation.
AI.result: Evaluated on seven embedded-system designs comprising 34 datasheets, the framework achieves 97.5% compatibility-verification accuracy and an 8.6× reduction in input context size compared to upload-and-query workflows.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate the feasibility of LLM-assisted, specification-based hardware compatibility verification at early design stages. They also highlight the substantial benefits of modular task decomposition, formalized verification criteria, and task-aware compact context construction in enabling trustworthy LLM-driven design automation.

title: ConfAL-WM: Confidence-Guided Active Learning for Action-Conditioned World Models
summary: Action-conditioned world models have become an important foundation for embodied prediction, planning, and synthetic data generation, but their errors under new task and scene distributions are often concentrated in localized spatiotemporal regions such as robot arms, manipulated objects, contact areas, and occluded objects. This paper presents ConfAL-WM, a confidence-guided active learning framework for post-training embodied world models. Built upon EVAC, we attach a lightweight confidence probe to UNet decoder features and predict dense confidence maps in the latent space. These maps are aggregated into task-, frame-, and patch-level scores, enabling both efficient data selection and localized training enhancement. Our pipeline first retrains the confidence probe and warms up EVAC with a small subset of target-domain data, then performs task-level prescreening to allocate sampling budgets, and finally applies selected-data retraining with optional frame or patch weighted data enhancement. Experiments on RoboTwin2.0 show that confidence-guided selection improves post-training efficiency, while dense frame and patch weighting further enhances prediction quality and embodied trajectory consistency compared with scalar reward, progress, and judge-based scoring baselines. A quick visual overview of this work is available at https://ConfAL-WM.github.io.

AI.tldr: ConfAL-WM is a confidence-guided active learning framework for post-training embodied world models. It uses a lightweight confidence probe on UNet decoder features to predict dense latent-space confidence maps, which are aggregated into task-, frame-, and patch-level scores for efficient data selection and localized training. Experiments on RoboTwin2.0 show improved post-training efficiency and prediction quality over scalar reward/progress/judge-based baselines.
AI.motivation: Action-conditioned world models fail under new task/scene distributions with errors concentrated in localized spatiotemporal regions (robot arms, manipulated objects, contact areas, occluded objects). Current post-training approaches lack targeted selection and enhancement of the most error-prone regions.
AI.method: Built on EVAC, ConfAL-WM attaches a lightweight confidence probe to UNet decoder features to predict dense confidence maps in latent space. These maps are aggregated into task-, frame-, and patch-level scores. The pipeline: (1) retrains the confidence probe and warms up EVAC on a small target-domain subset, (2) performs task-level prescreening for sampling budgets, (3) applies selected-data retraining with optional frame or patch weighted data enhancement.
AI.result: On RoboTwin2.0, confidence-guided selection improves post-training efficiency. Dense frame and patch weighting enhance prediction quality and embodied trajectory consistency compared to scalar reward, progress, and judge-based scoring baselines.
AI.conclusion: Confidence-guided active learning with dense spatiotemporal supervision provides a more effective and efficient post-training strategy for embodied world models, outperforming scalar-based scoring approaches.

title: FLARE: Verifying MILP Reformulations with LLM-Based Theorem Proving
summary: Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) is a fundamental tool for combinatorial optimization with extensive real-world applications. A central challenge is designing computationally efficient MILP formulations. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to automate the modeling process, from deriving formulations to strengthening them. Reliable automation requires robust methods for verifying that proposed formulations preserve the underlying optimization problem. However, existing approaches evaluate formulations numerically and fail to reason about general problem instances. We resolve this limitation by introducing a constructive definition of MILP reformulation that can be formalized in Lean and machine-checked. We develop FLARE (Formulation-Level Automated Reformulation Evaluation), a method that uses an LLM-based agent and the Lean proof assistant to verify proposed reformulations against a reference formulation. To evaluate our approach, we introduce FormulationBench, a challenging dataset of 20 problems and 109 formulations. FLARE outperforms existing methods, with 100% accuracy on the NP-hard subset of FormulationBench. Furthermore, FLARE produces a machine-checkable certificate for every reformulation it accepts. For cases where formal guarantees are not necessary, we introduce FLARE-NL, a fast and cheap LLM proxy that matches FLARE's accuracy but produces no certificate. These methods enable reliable verification in automated optimization modeling.

AI.tldr: FLARE introduces a constructive definition of MILP reformulation formalizable in the Lean proof assistant, enabling machine-checked verification of proposed MILP formulations. Combined with FLARE-NL, a faster LLM proxy, it achieves 100% accuracy on the NP-hard subset of FormulationBench, a new dataset of 20 problems and 109 formulations.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches for verifying MILP formulations evaluate them numerically and cannot reason about general problem instances, limiting the reliability of LLM-based automated optimization modeling. A robust, formally verifiable method for checking that proposed formulations preserve the underlying optimization problem is needed.
AI.method: FLARE uses an LLM-based agent combined with the Lean proof assistant to verify proposed reformulations against a reference formulation, based on a constructive definition of MILP reformulation formalized in Lean. FLARE-NL is a fast, cheap LLM proxy variant without certificate generation.
AI.result: On the new FormulationBench dataset (20 problems, 109 formulations), FLARE outperforms existing methods with 100% accuracy on the NP-hard subset, and produces a machine-checkable certificate for every accepted reformulation. FLARE-NL matches FLARE's accuracy without certificates.
AI.conclusion: Formal proof-based verification enables reliable verification in automated optimization modeling, offering both fully certified (FLARE) and fast proxy (FLARE-NL) options for different verification needs.

title: RA-VLA: Retrieval-Augmented VLA for Test-Time Adaptation
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models provide a versatile foundation for general robotic manipulation, yet they exhibit significant brittleness when confronted with novel task distributions. While In-Context Imitation Learning (ICIL) offers a training-free alternative, existing frameworks suffer from an adaptation bottleneck that hinders the effective translation of expert context to executable actions. This failure originates from superficial retrieval mechanisms and an inherent behavioral inertia that anchors the policy to its pre-trained priors. To address these limitations, we present RA-VLA, a retrieval-augmented VLA framework that integrates behavior-aligned context retrieval with a grounded execution pipeline. By enforcing faithful adherence to functional cues within a scalable architecture, RA-VLA facilitates seamless task adaptation while preserving inference efficiency. Our empirical evaluations across the LIBERO benchmark and a real-world UR5e environment demonstrate that RA-VLA achieves superior success rates and computational efficiency, establishing a robust framework for training-free robotic adaptation.

AI.tldr: RA-VLA is a retrieval-augmented Vision-Language-Action framework that addresses the adaptation bottleneck in in-context imitation learning by combining behavior-aligned context retrieval with a grounded execution pipeline, enabling training-free robotic task adaptation with high success rates and computational efficiency.
AI.motivation: VLA models are brittle when facing novel task distributions, and while In-Context Imitation Learning offers a training-free alternative, existing frameworks suffer from an adaptation bottleneck caused by superficial retrieval mechanisms and behavioral inertia that anchors policies to pre-trained priors.
AI.method: RA-VLA integrates behavior-aligned context retrieval with a grounded execution pipeline, enforcing faithful adherence to functional cues within a scalable architecture to facilitate seamless task adaptation while preserving inference efficiency.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations on the LIBERO benchmark and a real-world UR5e environment show that RA-VLA achieves superior success rates and computational efficiency compared to existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: RA-VLA establishes a robust framework for training-free robotic adaptation, overcoming the adaptation bottleneck in ICIL for VLAs by improving context retrieval and executing behaviors that faithfully align with retrieved functional cues.

title: Hierarchical MoE for Multi-Modal ILD Diagnosis
summary: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models combine specialized predictors under learned routing, offering a principled mechanism for leveraging heterogeneity in medical data. We present a hierarchical multimodal MoE for interstitial lung disease (ILD) classification that integrates a frozen, pre-trained imaging expert with structured electronic health records (EHR) via two-stage gating. A modality-level gate assigns patient-specific weights to imaging and EHR predictions, while a sub-gating module decomposes the EHR branch into clinically defined feature groups with learned, group-specific contributions. This design preserves stable imaging representations while enabling input-dependent clinical weighting and explicit EHR specialization. Under strict patient-level cross-validation, the model achieved the highest mean AUC among the evaluated methods (0.8750 +- 0.0443), compared with 0.8646 for imaging-only REN and 0.7685 for SwinUNETR. The framework extends interpretability across anatomical regions, imaging--EHR utilization, and clinically defined EHR feature groups.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical multimodal mixture-of-experts model for interstitial lung disease classification that integrates a frozen pre-trained imaging expert with structured EHR via two-stage gating (modality-level and sub-gating), achieving the highest mean AUC (0.8750 ± 0.0443) under strict patient-level cross-validation.
AI.motivation: MoE models offer a principled mechanism for leveraging heterogeneity in medical data, but applying them to multimodal medical data (imaging + EHR) has been underexplored. The authors aim to combine stable imaging representations with input-dependent clinical weighting for ILD classification.
AI.method: A hierarchical multimodal MoE with two-stage gating: (1) a modality-level gate assigns patient-specific weights to imaging and EHR predictions; (2) a sub-gating module decomposes the EHR branch into clinically defined feature groups with learned group-specific contributions. A frozen pre-trained imaging expert preserves stable representations.
AI.result: Under strict patient-level cross-validation, the model achieved the highest mean AUC (0.8750 ± 0.0443), outperforming imaging-only REN (0.8646) and SwinUNETR (0.7685). The framework extends interpretability across anatomical regions, imaging-EHR utilization, and clinically defined EHR feature groups.
AI.conclusion: The hierarchical multimodal MoE provides effective ILD classification by preserving stable imaging representations while enabling input-dependent clinical weighting and explicit EHR specialization, with enhanced interpretability across multiple dimensions.

title: Advantage-Driven Explicit Memory for Social Navigation
summary: Robot policies are predominantly learned with classical parametric variants of imitation learning or RL, where training stores the agent's behavior exclusively in the policy's network parameters, putting a heavy burden on the representation learning algorithm. We propose a new navigation agent equipped with non-parametric memory which explicitly indexes prior steps leading to critical events. The advantages are twofold: first, it allows the policy to outsource some of its behavior into an explicit memory; second, it encourages a form of continual learning by allowing an agent to collect data from its testing episodes during deployment and therefore to better generalize to OOD situations. In the context of social navigation, we show that this improves the agent's capability to retain sparse, high-cost failures, such as human collisions. If the policy is trained in simulation, this also naturally addresses the sim-to-real gap, partially, by basing some of the decision making on real data. We integrate the explicit memory into a recurrent PPO architecture and use hidden states for memory retrieval to capture continuous spatiotemporal dynamics. The goal of exploiting rare, high-impact events is achieved by leveraging the RL agent's advantage signals. We train our agent in simulation with a combination of photorealistic rendering and non-visual crowd simulation and show that the agent is robust with respect to OOD social behavior.

AI.tldr: A social navigation agent is proposed that augments a recurrent PPO policy with a non-parametric explicit memory which indexes prior steps leading to critical events (high-advantage states), allowing behavior outsourcing and continual learning during deployment, improving robustness to out-of-distribution social scenarios and partially addressing the sim-to-real gap.
AI.motivation: Classical parametric imitation learning and RL store all agent behavior solely in network parameters, placing a heavy burden on the representation learning algorithm. The authors aim to alleviate this by providing an explicit non-parametric memory and enabling continual learning from deployment data, particularly to capture sparse high-cost failures like human collisions.
AI.method: The agent uses a non-parametric memory that explicitly indexes prior steps leading to critical events, integrated into a recurrent PPO architecture. Hidden states are used for memory retrieval to capture continuous spatiotemporal dynamics, and advantage signals from RL are leveraged to identify rare, high-impact events worth storing. Training is performed in simulation using photorealistic rendering combined with non-visual crowd simulation.
AI.result: The explicit memory improves the agent's ability to retain sparse, high-cost failures (e.g., human collisions) and enhances robustness to out-of-distribution social behavior. Collecting data from testing episodes during deployment supports continual learning and improves generalization, while the use of real data in decision-making partially addresses the sim-to-real gap.
AI.conclusion: Outsourcing behavior into an explicit non-parametric memory, complemented by continual learning during deployment and advantage-based critical event selection, is an effective strategy for robust social navigation, especially under out-of-distribution conditions.

title: PhaseShift: Topology-Aware Data Harmonization and Model Consolidation Across Signalized Intersections
summary: Learned traffic-behavior models are commonly trained separately for each intersection, creating model portfolios that cannot share evidence across sites. We present PhaseShift, a topology-aware framework that harmonizes heterogeneous roadside trajectories into a shared actor-centric representation and trains one reusable backbone. Ego-relative coordinates, trajectory-induced movement paths, normalized signal context, and variable-cardinality interaction tokens remove site conventions while preserving behaviorally relevant topology. The backbone supports pooled operation, zero-shot at a held-out intersection, and low-data adaptation. We evaluate five intersections in two Florida regions on balanced field data, 100k training windows and equal-sized test sets per site under a replay-conditioned, best-of-sampled-trajectory protocol. At 10s, one pooled model lowers both minADE and minFDE relative to trained local models at all five sites, with median reductions of 36.8% and 22.0%. Leave-one-intersection-out deployment, including one cross-region fold, beats local training on both 10-s metrics at four of five sites, although short-horizon performance is less uniform. Fine-tuning with 1,000 target update windows improves on zero-shot at three sites and is the strongest regime at one. At site 7, every cross-site mixture sharply lowers long-horizon error under a fixed 100k-window budget; test-likelihood gains argue against a best-of-sample dispersion-only explanation. Local models fall behind calibrated IDM at the two highest-flow sites after long autoregressive rollouts; pretrained-backbone regimes do not. Within this five-site evaluation, PhaseShift demonstrates consolidation across heterogeneous physical control settings while identifying sites that still require adaptation. The protocol measures conditional single-vehicle generation under replayed context, not closed-loop traffic simulation.

AI.tldr: PhaseShift is a topology-aware framework that harmonizes heterogeneous roadside trajectories into a shared actor-centric representation, enabling a single reusable backbone to be pooled across intersections, zero-shot at held-out sites, and fine-tuned with limited data. Evaluated on five Florida intersections, it reduces median minADE by 36.8% and minFDE by 22.0% versus local models, while identifying sites that still require adaptation.
AI.motivation: Learned traffic-behavior models are typically trained separately per intersection, creating disjoint model portfolios that cannot share evidence across sites. This wastes data and prevents generalization across heterogeneous physical control settings.
AI.method: PhaseShift harmonizes heterogeneous roadside trajectories via ego-relative coordinates, trajectory-induced movement paths, normalized signal context, and variable-cardinality interaction tokens. This removes site conventions while preserving behaviorally relevant topology, enabling a single backbone to support pooled operation, zero-shot deployment, and low-data adaptation.
AI.result: On balanced field data from five intersections across two Florida regions (100k training windows, equal test sets), a single pooled model lowers both minADE and minFDE at all five sites versus trained local models, with median reductions of 36.8% and 22.0% at 10s. Leave-one-intersection-out deployment beats local training on both 10s metrics at four of five sites. Fine-tuning with 1,000 windows improves on zero-shot at three sites. Local models degrade at high-flow sites under long rollouts, while pretrained-backbone regimes remain stable.
AI.conclusion: PhaseShift demonstrates consolidation of traffic-behavior modeling across heterogeneous intersections through a shared, topology-aware representation. It identifies which sites can be served by a pooled or zero-shot backbone and which still require site-specific adaptation, while clarifying that the protocol measures conditional single-vehicle generation under replayed context rather than closed-loop simulation.

title: Leveraging Inter-object Affordances for Efficient Planning in Contact-rich Tasks
summary: Traditional task-and-motion planning (TAMP) approaches primarily focus on defining sequences of actions along with the necessary geometric and kinematic constraints to execute long-horizon tasks. However, their applicability in real-world settings is limited, as they typically assume simplified object models that overlook key physical properties critical for the successful execution of contact-rich tasks. Moreover, they often use sub-symbolic reasoning during motion planning, which drastically increases planning time and decreases overall success rates. We propose a method that leverages a TAMP approach, defining object-centric abstractions of execution constraints, called Unified TAMP (U-TAMP), to execute robotic tasks involving interactions among objects with heterogeneous shapes, sizes, and materials. Using a Vision-Language Model (VLM), we generate abstractions of inter-object affordances for characterizing physical interaction constraints between objects in contact-rich tasks, such as grasp and support constraints. These constraints are used to enrich the U-TAMP planning domain to deal with objects with variable physical properties. We perform experiments in simulated kitchen table organization scenarios and compare our results with those of the original U-TAMP, as well as a state-of-the-art VLM-based planner that leverages common sense knowledge of objects' affordances for plan generation. Our approach achieves significantly higher planning success rates and improves planning times by one to two orders of magnitude compared to other methods.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes U-TAMP, an extension of task-and-motion planning that uses a Vision-Language Model (VLM) to generate object-centric abstractions of inter-object affordances (grasp and support constraints), enabling TAMP to handle contact-rich tasks with heterogeneous object shapes, sizes, and materials. The method achieves significantly higher planning success rates and 1-2 orders of magnitude faster planning times compared to baselines in simulated kitchen table organization scenarios.
AI.motivation: Traditional TAMP methods are limited in real-world applicability because they assume simplified object models that ignore critical physical properties needed for contact-rich tasks, and they often rely on sub-symbolic reasoning during motion planning, which increases planning time and decreases success rates.
AI.method: The proposed method, Unified TAMP (U-TAMP), leverages a Vision-Language Model (VLM) to generate object-centric abstractions of inter-object affordances, characterizing physical interaction constraints (e.g., grasp and support constraints) between objects in contact-rich tasks. These constraints enrich the U-TAMP planning domain to handle objects with variable physical properties.
AI.result: Experiments in simulated kitchen table organization scenarios show the approach achieves significantly higher planning success rates and improves planning times by one to two orders of magnitude compared to the original U-TAMP and a state-of-the-art VLM-based planner using common sense knowledge of object affordances.
AI.conclusion: Integrating VLM-generated affordance abstractions into TAMP frameworks effectively addresses the challenges of contact-rich manipulation with heterogeneous objects, substantially improving both planning efficiency and success rates.

title: BixBench3: Benchmarking AI agents on research-study-scale computational biology tasks
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) promises to accelerate biological research by automating computational analyses. Yet the ability of AI agents to carry out computational biology at the scale of complete research studies has not been systematically evaluated. Here we introduce BixBench3, a benchmark that measures the capacity of AI agents to process raw biological data through to scientific results. We designed BixBench3 tasks to mirror the delegation of work from a scientist to an agent: the scientist chooses the research question and high-level methods, then delegates implementation of all analyses to the agent. In each task, an agent receives a research objective, methodological guidance, and raw data derived from a published scientific study, and must execute a sequence of analyses to achieve the research objective. The data artifacts resulting from these analyses - such as peak call matrices or differential expression tables - are programmatically graded against the corresponding artifacts generated and reported in the original study. Across 20 BixBench3 tasks encompassing the generation of 138 unique artifacts, we find that 13 frontier models achieve scores ranging from 0.00 for Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite to 0.48 for GPT 5.6 Sol. Agents perform worse on tasks with larger raw datasets (0.36 on tasks with <100 GB versus 0.10 on tasks with >100 GB) and on analyses requiring more sequential steps (0.36 at 1-2 steps vs 0.24 at 3+). On average, agents use 6.8 hours, 102 million tokens, and $43 to complete each task, with the longest attempts consuming 24 hours, 1.07 billion tokens, and $525. Notably, the highest-scoring agents used fewer tokens and were cheaper than less performant options. These results reveal that LLMs vary substantially in their ability to (1) execute multiple sequential analysis steps coherently, (2) manage large quantities of raw data, and (3) work across scientific domains.

AI.tldr: BixBench3 is a benchmark that evaluates the ability of AI agents to perform complete computational biology research studies, from raw data processing to scientific results. Across 20 tasks generating 138 artifacts, frontier models scored between 0.00 and 0.48, with performance degrading on large datasets (>100 GB) and multi-step analyses.
