Agents used substantial compute (up to 24 hours, 1.07B tokens, $525 per task), and top-scoring agents were actually more efficient than weaker ones.
AI.motivation: While AI agents have shown promise in automating computational analyses, their ability to carry out complete computational biology research studies at scale has not been systematically evaluated. Existing benchmarks do not capture the end-to-end delegation scenario where a scientist provides a research question and high-level methods, and an agent must execute all downstream analyses.
AI.method: The authors introduce BixBench3, a benchmark with 20 tasks derived from published scientific studies. Each task provides an agent with a research objective, methodological guidance, and raw data; agents must execute a sequence of analyses. The resulting data artifacts (e.g., peak call matrices, differential expression tables) are programmatically graded against artifacts from the original studies. Thirteen frontier models were evaluated across the tasks.

Performance dropped on large datasets (0.36 for <100 GB vs 0.10 for >100 GB) and on tasks requiring more sequential steps (0.36 at 1-2 steps vs 0.24 at 3+). Tasks averaged 6.8 hours, 102M tokens, and $43 per task. Notably, the highest-scoring agents used fewer tokens and were cheaper than less performant ones.
AI.conclusion: AI agents exhibit substantial variation in their capacity for coherent multi-step analysis execution, large-scale raw data management, and cross-domain scientific work. The benchmark reveals current limitations in end-to-end computational biology automation and indicates that efficiency and performance are not necessarily in tension—top models achieved better scores with lower resource consumption.

title: EgoNav: Bridging Learned Waypoints and Geometry-Aware Local Control for Robust Indoor Navigation
summary: Image-goal navigation using lightweight topological maps is a practical paradigm for indoor robot deployment: the map requires only geotagged images, and localization relies on visual matching rather than precise pose estimation. However, learned waypoint predictors can produce targets that violate geometric constraints or deviate from the global path. Executing these waypoints safely further requires a local planner capable of collision avoidance, yet existing systems either lack one or rely on fixed parameters that cannot adapt to confined spaces. To address these limitations while retaining the navigational intuition of the learned predictor, we present EgoNav, a hierarchical system that implements this idea by generating candidates from semantically segmented traversable regions and scoring them alongside the learned waypoint for geometric safety, directional coherence, and fidelity to the learned prior. An adaptive local path planner then executes the refined waypoint with parameters modulated based on the refinement outcome. Experiments in Habitat-sim and on a physical humanoid robot show that EgoNav consistently outperforms contemporary baselines in both success rate and path efficiency.

AI.tldr: EgoNav is a hierarchical navigation system for image-goal navigation that combines learned waypoint prediction with geometric constraint checking and an adaptive local planner, outperforming baselines in Habitat-sim and on a physical humanoid robot.
AI.motivation: Existing image-goal navigation systems using lightweight topological maps suffer from learned waypoint predictors that can violate geometric constraints or deviate from global paths, and either lack a local collision-avoidance planner or rely on fixed parameters that cannot adapt to confined spaces.
AI.method: EgoNav generates candidate waypoints from semantically segmented traversable regions and scores them alongside the learned waypoint to ensure geometric safety, directional coherence, and fidelity to the learned prior. An adaptive local path planner executes the refined waypoint with parameters modulated based on the refinement outcome.
AI.result: Experiments in Habitat-sim and on a physical humanoid robot show EgoNav consistently outperforms contemporary baselines in both success rate and path efficiency.
AI.conclusion: EgoNav demonstrates that augmenting a learned waypoint predictor with geometric refinement and an adaptive local planner enables safer and more efficient image-goal navigation in indoor environments, validated in both simulation and real-world deployment.

title: FinRiskAtlas: Decision-Aligned Evaluation of Large Language Models for Financial Risk Review
summary: Deploying large language models for professional financial review requires more than measuring general financial competence: models must perform the specific review operation required by a workflow and determine whether available evidence is sufficient for a defensible decision. Existing financial benchmarks cover knowledge, reasoning, compliance, and professional tasks, but their evaluation units are often organized around datasets or task formulations rather than the decisions that deployed systems support. We introduce FinRiskAtlas, a Chinese-language benchmark that evaluates financial LLMs along two complementary dimensions: operation execution under fixed evidence states and evidence-state control under evolving review conditions. The static benchmark contains 9,742 instances across 53 task families, including 42 Domain Knowledge families and eleven downstream review operations defined by explicit evaluation contracts. FinRisk-Ask extends this framework through offline replay of 680 pre-action states from 104 de-identified professional trajectories, withholding future evidence during inference and using it only to construct expert-verified evidence targets. Across 33 model configurations, operation-level evaluation yields non-redundant rankings (mean pairwise Spearman correlation 0.42 across downstream operations), and knowledge-based shortlisting can incur up to 18.01 points of regret on individual operations. FinRisk-Ask further shows that entering the Ask branch more frequently does not necessarily improve request targeting or end-to-end evidence acquisition. These results show that broad financial capability scores do not fully capture where models are reliable in professional workflows, motivating evaluation units aligned with the decisions and evidence states that deployed systems must support.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces FinRiskAtlas, a Chinese-language benchmark for evaluating financial LLMs along two dimensions: operation execution under fixed evidence states (static benchmark with 9,742 instances across 53 task families) and evidence-state control under evolving review conditions (FinRisk-Ask with offline replay of 680 pre-action states from 104 professional trajectories). Results across 33 model configurations show operation-level rankings are non-redundant (mean Spearman correlation 0.42), knowledge-based shortlisting can incur up to 18.01 points of regret, and more frequent Ask branching does not improve evidence targeting.
AI.motivation: Existing financial benchmarks evaluate LLMs around datasets or task formulations rather than the specific decisions and evidence states that deployed professional review systems must support, so broad financial competence scores do not capture where models are actually reliable in professional workflows.
AI.method: The benchmark is organized along two complementary dimensions: (1) a static benchmark of 9,742 instances across 53 task families (42 Domain Knowledge families and 11 downstream review operations defined by explicit evaluation contracts) for operation execution under fixed evidence states; and (2) FinRisk-Ask, which extends the framework via offline replay of 680 pre-action states from 104 de-identified professional trajectories, withholding future evidence during inference and using it only to construct expert-verified evidence targets for evidence-state control evaluation.
AI.result: Across 33 model configurations, operation-level evaluation yields non-redundant rankings (mean pairwise Spearman correlation 0.42 across downstream operations). Knowledge-based shortlisting can incur up to 18.01 points of regret on individual operations. FinRisk-Ask shows that entering the Ask branch more frequently does not necessarily improve request targeting or end-to-end evidence acquisition.
AI.conclusion: Broad financial capability scores do not fully capture where models are reliable in professional workflows, motivating evaluation units aligned with the decisions and evidence states that deployed systems must support.

title: GaussianDream++: Efficient 3D Gaussian World Modeling for Robotic Manipulation
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies have advanced language-conditioned robotic manipulation, yet action-imitation objectives provide only weak supervision for metric 3D structure and short-horizon physical evolution. Geometry-enhanced policies mainly improve current-scene grounding, whereas predictive policies often model future dynamics in RGB or latent spaces and may incur substantial deployment cost. GaussianDream demonstrates that training-time current Gaussian reconstruction and future Gaussian prediction provide effective 3D supervision, but its dense VGGT/TGE-based prefix jointly carries state, dynamics, and action-conditioning information. We present \textbf{\methodname}, a compact, policy-native extension that inserts \textbf{World State Tokens} and \textbf{World Prediction Tokens} directly into the VLA backbone. A training-only \textbf{World Representation Head} decodes these tokens into a Current World and coupled Future Prediction over shared Gaussian primitives, while static--dynamic factorization preserves persistent structure and focuses residual motion on interaction-relevant regions. At inference, the head, renderer, auxiliary objectives, and VGGT/TGE pathway are removed, leaving only 20 world tokens without online Gaussian decoding or rollout. \method achieves \textbf{98.6\%} on LIBERO and \textbf{87.8\%} on LIBERO-Plus, with clear gains under Camera and Layout shifts. Real-robot experiments further improve average success from 29.2\% to 52.5\% over reproduced $π_{0.5}$ while maintaining efficient closed-loop control.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a compact, policy-native extension for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies that inserts World State Tokens and World Prediction Tokens directly into the VLA backbone. A training-only World Representation Head decodes these tokens into current world and future prediction over shared Gaussian primitives, while static-dynamic factorization preserves structure and focuses residual motion. At inference, all auxiliary components are removed, leaving only 20 world tokens. The method achieves 98.6% on LIBERO, 87.8% on LIBERO-Plus, and improves real-robot success from 29.2% to 52.5% over reproduced π₀.₅.
AI.motivation: VLA policies using action-imitation objectives provide weak supervision for metric 3D structure and short-horizon physical evolution. Existing geometry-enhanced policies only improve current-scene grounding, while predictive policies model future dynamics in RGB or latent spaces at substantial deployment cost. This paper aims to provide effective 3D supervision (current Gaussian reconstruction + future Gaussian prediction) without incurring inference-time computational overhead.
AI.method: The method inserts World State Tokens and World Prediction Tokens directly into the VLA backbone. A training-only World Representation Head decodes these tokens into a Current World and coupled Future Prediction over shared Gaussian primitives. Static-dynamic factorization preserves persistent structure while focusing residual motion on interaction-relevant regions. At inference, the head, renderer, auxiliary objectives, and VGGT/TGE pathway are removed, leaving only 20 world tokens without online Gaussian decoding or rollout.
AI.result: Achieves 98.6% on LIBERO and 87.8% on LIBERO-Plus with clear gains under Camera and Layout shifts. Real-robot experiments improve average success from 29.2% to 52.5% over reproduced π₀.₅ while maintaining efficient closed-loop control.
AI.conclusion: Training-time Gaussian reconstruction and prediction provide effective 3D supervision for VLA policies, and this can be achieved through a compact, policy-native token design that is entirely removed at inference. The method demonstrates strong performance on benchmarks and real robots with minimal overhead, showing that world modeling can be effectively injected into VLA training without deployment cost.

title: Learning What to Share and What to Personalize: Hierarchical Strategy Co-Evolution for Agent Memory
summary: Memory-augmented agents maintain compact user profiles throughout extended conversations, enabling personalized and consistent responses without the need to process the entire dialogue history. The quality of these user profiles relies on the underlying memory management strategy: at each step, the agent must determine what to retain, compress, or discard. However, existing methods typically employ a static, one-size-fits-all strategy established before training. In practice, the optimal memory decision is inherently user-specific and dynamically evolves alongside policy optimization. To address this, we propose \textbf{HiPS} (\textbf{Hi}erarchical \textbf{P}ersonalized \textbf{S}trategy), a framework that decouples memory management into a globally shared foundation and a user-specific adaptive tier. Specifically, HiPS employs \textbf{Universal Strategy} to extract shared principles from cross-persona trajectories, alongside \textbf{Persona Delta Distillation} to generate tailored rules for users whose behaviors diverge from general patterns. \textbf{Cross-Level Rule Flow} dynamically calibrates their boundary by promoting broadly validated personal rules and demoting contradicted global ones. The architecture establishes a co-evolution loop where a mechanism guarantees that all strategy refinements are anchored to task outcomes. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements over memory-augmented baselines.

AI.tldr: HiPS is a hierarchical personalized memory management framework for memory-augmented agents, decoupling memory strategies into a globally shared foundation (Universal Strategy) and a user-specific adaptive tier (Persona Delta Distillation), with Cross-Level Rule Flow calibrating the boundary between them, leading to consistent improvements over baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing memory management strategies for augmented agents are static and one-size-fits-all, established before training. However, the optimal memory decision is inherently user-specific and dynamically evolves alongside policy optimization, necessitating a more adaptive approach.
AI.method: HiPS decouples memory management into two tiers: a globally shared foundation using Universal Strategy that extracts shared principles from cross-persona trajectories, and a user-specific adaptive tier via Persona Delta Distillation that generates tailored rules for users whose behaviors diverge from general patterns. Cross-Level Rule Flow dynamically calibrates the boundary between the two tiers by promoting broadly validated personal rules and demoting contradicted global ones, establishing a co-evolution loop anchored to task outcomes.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements over memory-augmented baselines.
AI.conclusion: A hierarchical, personalized approach to memory management—combining a shared global foundation with user-specific adaptation and dynamic calibration—outperforms static, one-size-fits-all strategies in memory-augmented agents.

title: PRISM: Projection-Integrated Sampling-Based MPC with Bayesian Cost Tuning for Bimanual Manipulation
summary:
Bimanual manipulation in cluttered, contact-rich environments remains challenging because it requires coordinated motion generation, interaction-aware planning, and reliable execution under tight kinematic constraints. We present PRISM, a projection-integrated sampling-based Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework that uses a GPU-accelerated physics simulator as an online world model for complex dual-arm manipulation.
  The main algorithmic contribution is a QP-guided control sampling strategy that decouples trajectory exploration from kinematic feasibility. At each MPC step, sampled joint-velocity trajectories are projected onto the set of motions satisfying joint position, velocity, acceleration, and jerk bounds, together with an initial-velocity boundary condition, before rollout evaluation. This enables broad yet feasible exploration of coordinated bimanual behaviors. To support efficient online execution, we derive a custom ADMM/Bregman-splitting QP solver that exploits joint-wise separability and reusable matrix factorizations. We further use Bayesian optimization to tune task-cost weights offline, reducing manual parameter selection.
  We evaluate PRISM on challenging variants of PerAct$^{2}$ tasks, including obstacle-constrained ball transport, tray transport, cube handover, and box lifting. Experiments show improved robustness and task success relative to representative sampling-based baselines, while maintaining real-time or near-real-time execution. We also demonstrate successful sim-to-real transfer on dual UR5e manipulators, highlighting the practical potential of physics-based online planning for contact-rich bimanual manipulation. Project details, including code and supplementary videos, are available at \href{https://sites.google.com/view/prismbimanual}{\texttt{https://sites.google.com/view/prismbimanual}}.

AI.tldr: PRISM is a projection-integrated sampling-based Model Predictive Control framework using a GPU-accelerated physics simulator as an online world model for dual-arm manipulation in cluttered, contact-rich environments. It uses QP-guided control sampling with an ADMM/Bregman-splitting solver for kinematic feasibility and Bayesian optimization for tuning task-cost weights, demonstrating improved robustness and real-time performance on challenging bimanual tasks with successful sim-to-real transfer on dual UR5e robots.
AI.motivation: Bimanual manipulation in cluttered, contact-rich environments remains challenging due to the need for coordinated motion generation, interaction-aware planning, and reliable execution under tight kinematic constraints. Existing methods struggle to simultaneously explore broad behaviors while maintaining feasibility during online planning.
AI.method: PRISM integrates a GPU-accelerated physics simulator as an online world model with a sampling-based MPC framework. The key algorithmic contribution is QP-guided control sampling that decouples trajectory exploration from kinematic feasibility by projecting sampled joint-velocity trajectories onto sets satisfying joint position, velocity, acceleration, and jerk bounds plus initial-velocity boundary conditions. A custom ADMM/Bregman-splitting QP solver exploits joint-wise separability and reusable matrix factorizations for efficient online execution. Bayesian optimization is used to tune task-cost weights offline.
AI.result: Evaluations on PerAct2 task variants (obstacle-constrained ball transport, tray transport, cube handover, box lifting) show improved robustness and task success over representative sampling-based baselines with real-time or near-real-time execution. Successful sim-to-real transfer is demonstrated on dual UR5e manipulators.
AI.conclusion: Physics-based online planning with projection-integrated sampling-based MPC is a practical and effective approach for contact-rich bimanual manipulation, achieving robust performance and sim-to-real viability.

title: Where vs What: Decomposing Structural and Content Failures in LLM-Generated Structured Outputs
summary: Structured outputs such as JSON and tables are central to modern LLM-based systems, yet generation failures are evaluated monolithically, conflating two distinct error modes: placement errors (correct values at wrong positions) and value errors (wrong values at intended positions). We introduce Structure-Content Decomposition (SCD), a framework that independently measures structural fidelity and content accuracy. Applying SCD to nested JSON and table tasks across six models (7B to frontier), we uncover a consistent phenomenon: structural fidelity degrades earlier and more sharply than content accuracy as complexity increases. At the highest complexity, even DeepSeek-V4-Flash (with reasoning) misplaces 35% of recalled values, while Qwen2.5-7B misplaces 74%. Controlled ablations suggest that this pattern is associated with reliance on semantic shortcuts rather than topological understanding of output structure. Based on these findings, we propose SA-RLVR, converting SCD metrics into verifiable rewards for reinforcement learning via GRPO. SA-RLVR successfully optimizes structural addressing across distinct topologies: it lifts JSON Value Placement Accuracy (VPA) from 26% to 63% while generalizing to held-out schemas; moreover, it consistently drives VPA improvements in the table domain, demonstrating that structure-aware rewards can directly enhance multi-domain structural positioning.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Structure-Content Decomposition (SCD), a framework that separately measures structural fidelity and content accuracy in structured LLM outputs. It finds that structural fidelity degrades earlier and more sharply than content accuracy with increasing complexity across six models, and proposes SA-RLVR, an RL method using SCD-based rewards that improves structural placement accuracy across JSON and table tasks.
AI.motivation: Structured output (JSON, tables) generation failures are currently evaluated monolithically, conflating two distinct error types: placement errors (correct values at wrong positions) and value errors (wrong values at intended positions). This conflation prevents targeted diagnosis and optimization of structural failures.
AI.method: (1) Introduces SCD, a decomposition framework that independently measures structural fidelity and content accuracy via metrics like Value Placement Accuracy (VPA). (2) Applies SCD to nested JSON and table tasks across six models (7B to frontier). (3) Conducts controlled ablations to investigate the cause of structural degradation. (4) Proposes SA-RLVR, converting SCD metrics into verifiable rewards for RL via GRPO.
AI.result: Structural fidelity degrades earlier and more sharply than content accuracy as complexity increases. At highest complexity, DeepSeek-V4-Flash misplaces 35% of recalled values while Qwen2.5-7B misplaces 74%. SA-RLVR lifts JSON VPA from 26% to 63% with generalization to held-out schemas, and consistently improves VPA in the table domain.
AI.conclusion: Structural failures in LLM structured generation are a distinct and more severe failure mode than content errors, linked to reliance on semantic shortcuts rather than topological understanding. Structure-aware rewards (SA-RLVR) can effectively optimize structural addressing and generalize across different output topologies and domains.

title: Opportunities of Self Supervised Learning for GNSS: Evaluation of a Deep Learning-Enhanced PVT Algorithm
summary: This work proposes a Deep Learning Enhanced PVT algorithm to mitigate multipath interference in dense urban areas. A supervised objective jointly predicts range corrections and uncertainty, while a JEPA-based self-supervised pretraining stage improves representation quality. The algorithm is evaluated over diverse driving scenarios, substantially improving PVT accuracy, particularly for unseen harsh urban conditions. These results highlight the potential of unlabelled GNSS data to improve generalization performance.

AI.tldr: A deep learning enhanced PVT (Position, Velocity, Time) algorithm that uses supervised joint prediction of range corrections and uncertainty, with JEPA-based self-supervised pretraining on unlabelled GNSS data, significantly improving PVT accuracy in dense urban multipath environments, especially under unseen harsh conditions.
AI.motivation: Multipath interference in dense urban areas severely degrades GNSS PVT accuracy. Existing approaches lack generalization to unseen harsh urban conditions, and there is untapped potential in unlabelled GNSS data to improve robustness.
AI.method: The approach combines a supervised objective that jointly predicts range corrections and uncertainty with a JEPA (Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture) based self-supervised pretraining stage to improve representation quality using unlabelled GNSS data.
AI.result: Evaluation across diverse driving scenarios demonstrates substantially improved PVT accuracy, with particularly strong gains on unseen harsh urban conditions, validating the generalization benefit of self-supervised pretraining on unlabelled data.
AI.conclusion: The results highlight the potential of leveraging unlabelled GNSS data through self-supervised learning to enhance generalization performance of deep learning based PVT algorithms in challenging urban environments.

title: Can your AI agent be cheaper? Investigating the effects of task specifications on token spend in agentic coding tasks
summary: Agentic coding workflows are now widely deployed in real-world systems. With long-horizon reasoning and tool use, token usage has become an important consideration for both cost and efficiency. Two engineers using AI will solve the same problem differently. How the specification of a task shapes an agent's token spend, and whether that spend can be predicted in advance, are open questions. Here, we study the effects of different task specifications on agentic token spend with the Kimi K3 model at three thinking efforts. Across $2,700$ runs, we show that reducing a full task specification to a bare user story raises token spend by $29.7\%$, while run-to-run variance remains unaffected by any prompt changes. We show that prompt-sensitivity is task-dependent, running from $13\%$ to $115\%$. We fit a simple predictor that can price a full distribution of task specifications and thinking effort configurations from a single cheap probe on an unseen task within $36\%$, improving over prior work in predicting token spend. Our work provides initial results quantifying the effects of task specification on agentic token spend and introduces a method that can be used to systematically evaluate the cost of AI coding workflows.

AI.tldr: This paper quantifies how task specification affects token spend in agentic coding workflows using the Kimi K3 model across 2,700 runs. It finds that reducing a full task specification to a bare user story increases token spend by 29.7%, that prompt-sensitivity varies from 13% to 115% depending on the task, and proposes a simple predictor that can estimate token spend distributions for unseen tasks within 36% accuracy from a single cheap probe.
AI.motivation: With the widespread deployment of agentic coding workflows, token usage has become a critical cost and efficiency concern. However, whether task specification shapes an agent's token spend and whether this spend can be predicted in advance remain open questions.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic study with the Kimi K3 model at three thinking efforts, running 2,700 total runs. They manipulate task specifications (from full specifications down to bare user stories) and compare token spend. They also fit a simple predictor on an unseen task from a single cheap probe to price the full distribution of task specifications and thinking effort configurations.
AI.result: Reducing a full task specification to a bare user story increases token spend by 29.7%, while run-to-run variance is unaffected by prompt changes. Prompt-sensitivity is task-dependent, ranging from 13% to 115%. The proposed predictor estimates token spend distributions on unseen tasks within 36% accuracy, improving over prior work.
AI.conclusion: The work provides initial quantitative results on how task specification affects agentic token spend and introduces a method for systematically evaluating the cost of AI coding workflows.

title: LM-X: Explainable Action Modeling with Progress, Event, and Uncertainty Prediction for Generalist Robot Manipulation
summary: Generalist vision--language--action (VLA) policies learn long-horizon behavior mainly through short-horizon action prediction and reveal little beyond sampled commands. This creates two coupled bottlenecks: a single action target must implicitly absorb task progress, intermediate intent, and local reliability, while these control states remain hidden during execution. Inspired by functional principles of biological sensorimotor control, we introduce LM-X , which organizes prediction across task, event, and motor scales without claiming anatomical correspondence. Three explicitly supervised signals are emitted online and directly condition action generation: return-to-go (RTG) measures visible task progress, event-to-go (ETG) identifies the next semantic transition, and heteroscedastic action flow estimates local reliability through propagated variance. Explanation is therefore intrinsic to control rather than generated post hoc. Before a costly 20-day pretraining run on 64 NVIDIA B200 GPUs, a controlled five-task pretraining gate verifies the design: the complete model improves success by 16.0 points over the action-only backbone and by 10.8 points over the strongest single-head variant. We then train LM-X on more than 20,000 hours of real-robot trajectories, including over 1,000 hours of failed policy rollouts. LM-X achieves 74.1\% across 50 randomized-hard RoboTwin2.0 tasks versus 55.4\% for GR00T N1.7, and 68.6\% versus 50.7\% across seven real-robot tasks. RTG tracks semantic progress and visible regression, while variance rises during hesitation and oscillatory control. These results show that explicit multi-timescale predictive state can strengthen control while exposing interpretable internal estimates.

AI.tldr: LM-X is a generalist vision-language-action (VLA) policy that emits three explicitly supervised multi-timescale predictive signals—return-to-go (RTG), event-to-go (ETG), and heteroscedastic action flow (variance)—that directly condition action generation, making explanation intrinsic to control. Trained on 20,000+ hours of real-robot data (including 1,000+ hours of failed rollouts), LM-X achieves 74.1% success across 50 RoboTwin2.0 tasks (vs. 55.4% for GR00T N1.7) and 68.6% across seven real-robot tasks (vs. 50.7%).
AI.motivation: Standard VLA policies predict short-horizon actions while hidden control states (task progress, intermediate intent, local reliability) are implicitly absorbed into a single action target, creating coupled bottlenecks: action prediction must simultaneously encode multiple latent states while those states remain unobservable during execution.
AI.method: LM-X organizes prediction across task, event, and motor scales, emitting three online supervised signals that directly condition action generation: RTG (visible task progress), ETG (next semantic transition), and heteroscedastic action flow (local reliability via propagated variance). A controlled five-task pretraining gate validates the design before the full 20-day pretraining on 64 NVIDIA B200 GPUs, followed by training on 20,000+ hours of real-robot trajectories including 1,000+ hours of failed policy rollouts.
AI.result: The complete model improves success by 16.0 points over the action-only backbone and 10.8 points over the strongest single-head variant in the pretraining gate. Across 50 randomized-hard RoboTwin2.0 tasks, LM-X achieves 74.1% vs. 55.4% for GR00T N1.7; across seven real-robot tasks, 68.6% vs. 50.7%. RTG tracks semantic progress while variance rises during hesitation and oscillatory control.
AI.conclusion: Explicit multi-timescale predictive state can strengthen control while exposing interpretable internal estimates, demonstrating that explanation intrinsic to control outperforms post hoc generation and that biological-inspired multi-scale prediction benefits generalist robot policies.

title: Paint What You See: Benchmarking Dexterous Visual Tool Use in Multimodal Agents
summary: Evaluation is shifting from static QA toward agentic settings where models act through external tools. We identify a critical yet underexplored capability within this space - dexterous visual tool use: fine-grained, closed-loop parameterized visual action in which models infer tool parameters from visual evidence, and those parameters directly govern the final result. Existing benchmarks cover web navigation, GUI operation, and software engineering, but rarely target this coupling between visual evidence and execution precision. We propose EASEL, a benchmark evaluating a controlled instance of dexterous visual tool use that adopts reference-guided visual reconstruction as its primary proxy task: the agent incrementally paints a canvas to match a reference image. EASEL additionally includes semantic tasks spanning region annotation, handwriting, and path planning. We further provide EASEL-Data, a 440k-sample two-stage curriculum dataset for trajectory supervision, and EASEL-9B to investigate its effect on this capability. Evaluation of 25 models reveals that current multimodal agents systematically struggle on EASEL. Reconstruction similarity bottlenecks at low levels (0.40-0.54), while trajectory diagnostics expose severe closed-loop instability - models typically saturate early or degrade post-peak. Semantic tasks reveal sharp capability boundaries in precision annotation and path planning. EASEL-9B, trained on EASEL-Data, surpasses the base model by a relative 6.3%, ranking third among all evaluated models.

AI.tldr: EASEL is a benchmark for evaluating dexterous visual tool use—fine-grained, closed-loop parameterized visual actions where models infer tool parameters from visual evidence. Using reference-guided visual reconstruction (incremental canvas painting) as a proxy task, plus semantic tasks (region annotation, handwriting, path planning), the paper also introduces EASEL-Data (440k-sample curriculum) and EASEL-9B. Evaluation of 25 models shows systematic failures in reconstruction (0.40-0.54 similarity), closed-loop instability, and semantic task boundaries; EASEL-9B improves the base by 6.3% relative.
AI.motivation: Evaluation is moving toward agentic settings, but existing benchmarks (web navigation, GUI operation, software engineering) rarely target the coupling between visual evidence and execution precision. The paper identifies dexterous visual tool use as a critical, underexplored capability and aims to systematically evaluate and improve it.
AI.method: The paper proposes EASEL, a benchmark built on reference-guided visual reconstruction as the proxy task (agent incrementally paints to match a reference image), augmented with semantic tasks including region annotation, handwriting, and path planning. It provides EASEL-Data, a 440k-sample two-stage curriculum dataset for trajectory supervision, and trains EASEL-9B on this data.
AI.result: Across 25 models, multimodal agents systematically struggle: reconstruction similarity caps at 0.40-0.54; trajectory diagnostics reveal closed-loop instability (saturation or post-peak degradation); semantic tasks expose sharp performance boundaries. EASEL-9B surpasses its base model by 6.3% relative and ranks third among all evaluated models.
AI.conclusion: Current multimodal agents lack dexterous visual tool use capability, and existing benchmarks fail to measure it. EASEL provides a controlled evaluation framework, and curriculum-based training (EASEL-Data/EASEL-9B) demonstrates measurable improvement, suggesting this capability can be enhanced through targeted data and training while remaining challenging.

title: TacForcing: Streaming Action Generation with Execution-Time Tactile Feedback
summary: Contact-rich manipulation requires adapting to contact states that can evolve substantially within an action horizon. However, chunk-based vision-language-action models predict complete action chunks from observations collected before execution, leaving tactile conditioning stale during execution. Existing tactile-reactive approaches typically rely on separate high-frequency controllers, which increase both architectural and training complexity. In this paper, we introduce TacForcing, a streaming action-generation framework that effectively incorporates execution-time tactile feedback. Instead of employing a separate reactive controller, TacForcing replaces the standard action expert with a streaming action expert to generate actions conditioned on the evolving tactile observations acquired during execution. TacForcing also introduces Execution-Aware Tactile Attention (EATA), which restricts tactile conditioning to actions nearing execution, thereby reducing the temporal mismatch between tactile acquisition and action execution. Across six simulated UniVTAC tasks and three real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, TacForcing achieves average success rates of 65% and 69%, respectively, outperforming strong baselines in both settings.

AI.tldr: TacForcing is a streaming action-generation framework that incorporates execution-time tactile feedback into vision-language-action models for contact-rich manipulation, replacing separate reactive controllers with a streaming action expert and using Execution-Aware Tactile Attention (EATA) to reduce temporal mismatch between tactile acquisition and action execution.
AI.motivation: Chunk-based vision-language-action models predict complete action chunks before execution, causing tactile conditioning to become stale during execution. Existing tactile-reactive approaches rely on separate high-frequency controllers, increasing architectural and training complexity.
AI.method: TacForcing replaces the standard action expert with a streaming action expert that generates actions conditioned on evolving tactile observations acquired during execution. It introduces Execution-Aware Tactile Attention (EATA), which restricts tactile conditioning to actions nearing execution to reduce temporal mismatch.
AI.result: Across six simulated UniVTAC tasks and three real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, TacForcing achieves average success rates of 65% and 69%, respectively, outperforming strong baselines in both settings.
AI.conclusion: TacForcing effectively integrates execution-time tactile feedback into a streaming action-generation framework, achieving superior performance over baselines in both simulated and real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks without requiring a separate reactive controller.

title: Distance Is Not Enough: Forget-Retain Alignment Gap Predicts LLM Relearning Robustness
summary: Machine unlearning aims to make a model forget specific data, yet unlearned LLMs often fail to stay unlearned: brief fine-tuning can revive removed knowledge. Existing robustness predictors rely on global weight-space displacement, but distance alone can be misleading when random or destructive updates collapse performance. We argue that relearning robustness depends on update structure: robust unlearning should affect forget-critical weights while sparing retain-critical ones. We introduce the Forget-Retain Alignment Gap (FRAG), a training-free predictor that scores an update's forget-retain alignment without running a relearning attack, and separates selective from dense updates more reliably than global distance. Building on the forget-critical, retain-sparing principle, Forget-Retain Pruning (FRP) improves relearning robustness. Our results suggest that weight selectivity better explains robustness than distance alone. Code is available at https://github.com/Yi1-Chen/FRAG.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes that relearning robustness in unlearned LLMs depends not on global weight-space displacement but on the structural alignment of updates with forget-critical versus retain-critical weights. It introduces FRAG, a training-free predictor of forget-retain alignment, and FRP, a pruning method that improves robustness by selectively modifying forget-critical weights while sparing retain-critical ones.
AI.motivation: Unlearned LLMs frequently fail to stay unlearned—brief fine-tuning can revive removed knowledge. Existing robustness predictors based on global weight-space displacement are unreliable because distance alone is misleading when random or destructive updates collapse performance, indicating the need for a more structure-aware predictor.
AI.method: The authors define the concept of update structure, arguing that robust unlearning should affect forget-critical weights while sparing retain-critical ones. They introduce the Forget-Retain Alignment Gap (FRAG), a training-free score that measures an update's forget-retain alignment without requiring a relearning attack, plus Forget-Retain Pruning (FRP) which operationalizes the forget-critical, retain-sparing principle.
AI.result: FRAG separates selective updates from dense updates more reliably than global distance, and FRP improves relearning robustness of unlearned models. Results indicate that weight selectivity explains relearning robustness better than distance alone.
AI.conclusion: Relearning robustness in machine unlearning is better explained by the structural alignment of weight updates with forget-critical and retain-critical parameters than by global weight-space displacement. FRAG and FRP provide practical, training-free tools for predicting and improving this robustness.

title: AGRO-Nav: Autonomous Graph-based Orchard Navigation
summary: Orchards form semi-structured environments in which parallel tree rows create natural driving corridors, yet narrow inter-row clearance and dense foliage lead geometry-agnostic grid planners to drift off the row center and risk trunk or canopy contact. We present AGRO-Nav, an automated framework for static graph-based global planning in orchards. From tree-row lines fitted to trunk clusters in a SLAM point cloud, it builds, without any manual waypoints, a sparse topological graph of intra- and inter-row connectivity; a global route is then found by Dijkstra search on this graph, connected to the start and goal by any-angle Theta* segments, and smoothed with a cubic B-spline. In real-orchard trials, AGRO-Nav follows the row center with a mean error of about 0.08 m, far below the A* (0.31 m) and Theta* (0.43 m) shortest-path baselines, while planning roughly four to five times faster. In Isaac Sim, it attains the lowest error among A*, Theta*, and a reproduced RANSAC midline baseline and remains stable as tree density drops to 70%, where the RANSAC baseline degrades. The resulting trajectories---straight row-centered segments joined by controlled turns---suit differential-drive and four-wheel-steering platforms.

AI.tldr: AGRO-Nav is an automated framework for static graph-based global planning in orchards that builds a sparse topological graph from SLAM point cloud tree-row lines, enabling row-centered navigation via Dijkstra search with Theta* connections and B-spline smoothing. It achieves ~0.08 m mean row-center error in real orchards and remains robust in simulation even with reduced tree density, significantly outperforming A*, Theta*, and RANSAC baselines in both accuracy and planning speed.
AI.motivation: Orchard environments have narrow inter-row clearances and dense foliage that cause geometry-agnostic grid planners (e.g., A*) to drift from the row center, risking trunk or canopy collisions. Existing methods fail to exploit the semi-structured parallel tree-row layout for reliable, centered global planning.
AI.method: AGRO-Nav fits tree-row lines to trunk clusters in a SLAM point cloud, builds a sparse topological graph of intra- and inter-row connectivity without manual waypoints, finds a global route via Dijkstra search on the graph, connects start/goal via any-angle Theta* segments, and smooths the path with cubic B-splines.
AI.result: In real-orchard trials, AGRO-Nav achieves a mean row-center error of ~0.08 m, far below A* (0.31 m) and Theta* (0.43 m), with 4-5x faster planning. In Isaac Sim, it has the lowest error among all baselines and remains stable at 70% tree density, where the RANSAC baseline degrades. Trajectories consist of straight row-centered segments joined by controlled turns, suitable for differential-drive and four-wheel-steering platforms.
AI.conclusion: AGRO-Nav demonstrates that exploiting orchard-specific topological structure enables accurate, fast, and robust global planning that keeps vehicles centered in rows and outperforms general-purpose shortest-path planners and midline-estimation baselines in both real and simulated settings.

title: Training Alignment Auditors via Reinforcement Learning
comment: 82 pages, 15 figures. Code, prompts, and evaluation data are available at https://github.com/paulrosu11/training-auditing-agents-public
summary: Alignment auditing of frontier models increasingly relies on LLM auditors to surface undesirable behaviors at scale, but current automated auditors can struggle with coherent investigation and audit realism. In this work, we improve LLM auditors with reinforcement learning. In our best training environment, the policy investigates target models that potentially possess hidden behaviors planted via their system prompt. An LLM judge, which knows whether the target has a hidden behavior, holistically compares the policy's investigation to a reference investigation to determine the reward. With systematic ablations, we find that pairwise rewards yield more robust training compared to pointwise rewards, and that adding targets without planted behaviors helps maintain a low false positive rate. Training improves investigation quality against targets with planted behaviors, the rate of concerning behaviors surfaced in unmodified production models, and audit realism, while false-positive rates stay below 1%. Furthermore, auditing capabilities generalize across scaffolds: performance on AuditBench's adversarially fine-tuned targets substantially improves [Sheshadri et al., 2026].

AI.tldr: This paper improves LLM auditors using reinforcement learning, where a policy investigates target models that may have hidden behaviors planted via system prompts. Training with pairwise rewards and including targets without planted behaviors (to maintain low false positives) improves investigation quality, audit realism, and generalization across scaffolds, with false-positive rates staying below 1%.
AI.motivation: Current automated LLM auditors struggle with coherent investigation and audit realism when surfacing undesirable behaviors in frontier models at scale.
AI.method: The policy is trained in an environment where it investigates target models that may have hidden behaviors planted via their system prompts. An LLM judge, aware of whether the target has a hidden behavior, holistically compares the policy's investigation to a reference investigation to determine reward. Systematic ablations show pairwise rewards are more robust than pointwise rewards, and adding targets without planted behaviors helps maintain low false positive rates.
AI.result: Training improves investigation quality against targets with planted behaviors, increases the rate of concerning behaviors surfaced in unmodified production models, and improves audit realism, while false-positive rates stay below 1%. Auditing capabilities also generalize across scaffolds, substantially improving performance on AuditBench's adversarially fine-tuned targets.
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement learning with pairwise rewards and a mix of targets with and without planted behaviors produces more effective and realistic LLM auditors with low false positive rates, and capabilities transfer to new evaluation settings.

title: Anytime Global Tensor Motion Planning
summary: Global Tensor Motion Planning (GTMP) solves motion planning with batched tensor operations over a layered multipartite graph. We generalize GTMP so that adjacent-layer edges are realized by any black-box local planner (e.g., linear interpolation, splines, sampling-based planning, trajectory optimization, or generative sampling). We provide two anytime policies on top of this generalization: Anytime GTMP with random restarts at a fixed budget, which covers every homotopy class almost surely, and AO-GTMP with informed expansion with growing budgets, which converges to the optimal cost. We prove that a single sampled graph covers every endpoint-fixed homotopy class admitting a \(δ\)-clear representative of bounded length. We also prove that additional samples per layer reduce the per-layer miss probability exponentially, whereas stronger local planners reduce the required layer count only sublinearly. On manipulation benchmarks the method matches state-of-the-art performance, and on 2D navigation it returns batches of topologically diverse solutions, while the informed baselines concentrate on one or two classes.

AI.tldr: This paper generalizes Global Tensor Motion Planning (GTMP) to support any black-box local planner between adjacent layers in a layered multipartite graph, and introduces two anytime policies: one with random restarts at fixed budget covering all homotopy classes almost surely, and AO-GTMP with informed expansion converging to optimal cost. The paper proves coverage guarantees for sampled graphs and efficiency bounds relating sample count and local planner strength to performance.
AI.motivation: Extend GTMP beyond specific local planners so that arbitrary planners (interpolation, splines, sampling-based, trajectory optimization, or generative sampling) can be used, while providing anytime operation and theoretical guarantees on homotopy class coverage and optimality convergence.
AI.method: Generalizes GTMP to allow any black-box local planner for adjacent-layer edges; proposes Anytime GTMP with random restarts at fixed budget and AO-GTMP with informed expansion and growing budgets; provides proofs on homotopy class coverage for a single sampled graph and on exponential reduction of per-layer miss probability with more samples versus sublinear layer-count reduction with stronger local planners.
AI.result: On manipulation benchmarks the method matches state-of-the-art performance; on 2D navigation it returns batches of topologically diverse solutions while informed baselines concentrate on one or two homotopy classes.
AI.conclusion: The generalized GTMP framework enables anytime, topologically diverse motion planning with arbitrary local planners, offering strong theoretical guarantees and competitive empirical performance while overcoming the subset focus of informed baselines.

title: PonsRAG: A Pons-Inspired RAG Bridging Cognitive Islands for Coordinated Long Narrative Reasoning
summary: Long Narrative Reasoning is an essential capability for processing and reasoning over complex narratives. While retrieval-augmented generation provides a promising framework, existing methods still face two critical challenges: cognitive islanding and cross-layer evidence disconnection. To address these issues, we propose PonsRAG, a coordinated RAG framework inspired by the biological pons. PonsRAG consists of two key components: Triple-Layer Indexing, which organizes documents into a connected knowledge structure to bridge cognitive islands, and Coordinated Reasoning, which retrieves evidence across distinct layers and integrates cross-layer information into a unified context. We evaluate PonsRAG on four long-context narrative benchmarks, and experimental results show that it outperforms the strongest baseline, achieving a 11.56% relative improvement in average accuracy on multi-choice tasks.

AI.tldr: PonsRAG is a coordinated retrieval-augmented generation framework inspired by the biological pons, designed to address cognitive islanding and cross-layer evidence disconnection in long narrative reasoning. It achieves an 11.56% relative improvement over the strongest baseline on four long-context narrative benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG methods for long narrative reasoning suffer from two critical challenges: cognitive islanding (fragmented understanding of disconnected narrative segments) and cross-layer evidence disconnection (inability to link evidence across different levels of narrative structure).
AI.method: PonsRAG comprises two key components: (1) Triple-Layer Indexing, which organizes documents into a connected knowledge structure to bridge cognitive islands, and (2) Coordinated Reasoning, which retrieves evidence across distinct layers and integrates cross-layer information into a unified context.
AI.result: Evaluated on four long-context narrative benchmarks, PonsRAG outperforms the strongest baseline with an 11.56% relative improvement in average accuracy on multi-choice tasks.
AI.conclusion: The coordinated RAG framework effectively resolves the cognitive islanding and cross-layer evidence disconnection problems, demonstrating significant gains in long narrative reasoning performance.

title: MA-VLA: Multi-Arm Vision-Language-Action Model for Collaboration and Compositional Generalization
summary: Multi-arm collaboration is becoming a core capability in embodied manipulation. Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models integrate perception, language, and control, but most represent language as a single global instruction and do not provide an explicit mechanism for assigning and composing arm-specific behaviors. This design limits transfer to collaboration patterns that differ from those observed during training. We present MA-VLA, a unified framework for multi-arm collaboration via atomic action assignment. MA-VLA decomposes cooperative behavior into mid-level atomic prompts and allocates them to individual arms, enabling explicit subgoal specification and compositional reuse across tasks. To reduce reliance on fixed execution roles, we introduce Arm Shuffle, a training-time permutation of the observation, state, and assigned atomic prompts for each arm. This permutation enforces role-agnostic instruction following and supports recomposition into unseen coordination patterns, which we term multi-arm compositional generalization. We also construct a benchmark in which test-time collaboration patterns are absent in training set. Across simulation and real-world evaluations, prior state-of-the-art VLAs largely fail under these unseen collaborations, while MA-VLA consistently succeeds. These results indicate that structured, per-arm atomic action assignment offers a practical route to scalable generalization in multi-arm embodied systems. Code, models, and data are available at https://github.com/zhangzaibin/future-robots

AI.tldr: MA-VLA is a unified framework for multi-arm robot collaboration that decomposes cooperative behaviors into per-arm atomic prompt assignments, enabling compositional generalization to unseen coordination patterns. It introduces Arm Shuffle (training-time permutation of observations and prompts) to enforce role-agnostic instruction following, and demonstrates success where prior state-of-the-art VLAs fail in both simulation and real-world benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA models for multi-arm manipulation treat language as a single global instruction without explicit mechanisms for assigning and composing arm-specific behaviors. This limits generalization to collaboration patterns not seen during training, hindering scalability to flexible multi-arm coordination in embodied manipulation.
AI.method: MA-VLA decomposes cooperative behavior into mid-level atomic prompts allocated to individual arms for explicit subgoal specification and compositional reuse. It introduces Arm Shuffle, a training-time permutation of observation, state, and assigned atomic prompts per arm, which enforces role-agnostic instruction following and enables recomposition into unseen coordination patterns (multi-arm compositional generalization). A benchmark is constructed where test-time collaboration patterns are absent from the training set.
AI.result: In simulation and real-world evaluations, prior state-of-the-art VLA models largely fail under unseen collaboration patterns, while MA-VLA consistently succeeds, demonstrating robust multi-arm compositional generalization.
AI.conclusion: Structured, per-arm atomic action assignment offers a practical and scalable route to generalization in multi-arm embodied systems, opening avenues for flexible coordination beyond training-observed patterns.

title: CaSKG: Counterfactual-Causal Skill Graphs for Scalable Agent Skill Retrieval
summary: Reusable skill libraries allow large language model (LLM) agents to reuse procedural knowledge across tasks, but they also turn memory access into a challenging retrieval problem. Full-library prompting preserves coverage at high context cost, vector retrieval returns compact neighborhoods but treats skills as independent text, and graph-based retrieval can recover workflow context only when the edges that carry relevance are reliable. We propose CaSKG, a counterfactual-causal skill graph framework that calibrates procedural relations before retrieval. CaSKG first builds a high-recall directed candidate graph from semantic, lexical, input/output, and structural evidence, with repair evidence and an optional LLM judge further refining candidate scores. It then applies direction-conditioned textual counterfactual probes that remove, substitute, and reorder skill pairs, aggregates the evidence with Bayesian smoothing, and publishes a state-filtered weighted graph for task-conditioned expansion. The graph is constructed offline and used without changing the downstream agent policy or task interface. Across six LLM backbones on ALFWorld ID-140 and ScienceWorld U211, CaSKG achieves the highest task score in all twelve combinations of model and benchmark. Relative to Graph-of-Skills (GoS), it improves the six-model macro-average ScienceWorld score from 72.62 to 80.50 and ALFWorld success from 80.01\% to 86.79\%, while reducing mean environment steps on both benchmarks. Qualitative and ablation analyses further show that calibrated edges help retrieval preserve prerequisites, state-changing actions, verification routines, and final completion steps. These results position edge-confidence calibration as an effective route to compact and executable skill retrieval at scale\footnote{Code is available at: https://github.com/ZhiyuanLi218/Caskg }.

AI.tldr: CaSKG is a counterfactual-causal skill graph framework that calibrates procedural relations between skills before retrieval, using direction-conditioned textual counterfactual probes (removal, substitution, reordering) and Bayesian smoothing to build a weighted graph, achieving state-of-the-art task scores across six LLM backbones on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LLM agents reuse procedural knowledge via reusable skill libraries, but memory retrieval is challenging: full-library prompting has high context costs, vector retrieval treats skills as independent text ignoring workflows, and graph-based retrieval relies on unreliable edges.
AI.method: CaSKG first builds a high-recall directed candidate graph from semantic, lexical, input/output, and structural evidence with repair evidence and optional LLM judge refining scores. It then applies direction-conditioned textual counterfactual probes (remove, substitute, reorder skill pairs), aggregates evidence with Bayesian smoothing, and publishes a state-filtered weighted graph for task-conditioned expansion, constructed offline without changing the downstream agent policy.
AI.result: Across six LLM backbones on ALFWorld ID-140 and ScienceWorld U211, CaSKG achieves the highest task score in all twelve model/benchmark combinations. vs GoS, ScienceWorld score improves from 72.62 to 80.50 and ALFWorld success from 80.01% to 86.79%, while reducing mean environment steps on both benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Edge-confidence calibration in skill graphs is an effective route to compact and executable skill retrieval at scale; calibrated edges help preserve prerequisites, state-changing actions, verification routines, and final completion steps.

title: VISTA: Visually Inferred Spatial ConTact Attention for Contact-Rich Manipulation
summary: Contact-rich manipulation requires precise interaction feedback. While vision-centric imitation learning is prevalent, external visual observations provide indirect and ambiguous cues about contact states, particularly under occlusion or subtle object--gripper interactions; dedicated tactile or force sensors can provide rich contact information but introduce additional hardware complexity, calibration requirements, and deployment costs. To bridge this gap, we propose VISTA-Policy, an imitation learning paradigm that utilizes the Visual Deformation Field (VDF), a 3D displacement representation of a compliant gripper, as high-dimensional visuo-physical feedback. The framework integrates: 1) a Physics-Aware Encoding Engine for real-time VDF decoding; 2) an Energy Aggregation Denoising Mechanism to isolate true interaction signals; and 3) a Deformation-Augmented Policy Network with incremental gripper actions for precise closed-loop correction. Extensive evaluations on Cross-Scale Object Grasping, Cap Unscrewing, and Calligraphy Writing demonstrate that VISTA-Policy outperforms the strong pure-vision baseline 3D Diffusion Policy and the tactile baseline. VISTA-Policy further demonstrates substantial out-of-distribution generalization to unseen object scales and robustness against dynamic disturbances, offering a durable and cost-effective route toward general-purpose fine-grained manipulation in unstructured environments. Project videos and supplementary materials are available at: https://sites.google.com/view/vista-policy.

AI.tldr: VISTA-Policy is an imitation learning paradigm that leverages a Visual Deformation Field (VDF) of a compliant gripper as high-dimensional visuo-physical feedback for contact-rich manipulation, integrating a Physics-Aware Encoding Engine, Energy Aggregation Denoising, and a Deformation-Augmented Policy Network. It outperforms both pure-vision (3D Diffusion Policy) and tactile baselines across grasping, cap unscrewing, and calligraphy tasks, with strong out-of-distribution generalization and robustness.
AI.motivation: Vision-centric imitation learning provides indirect and ambiguous contact cues under occlusion or subtle interactions, while tactile/force sensors offer rich contact information but introduce hardware complexity, calibration overhead, and deployment costs. A cost-effective, high-fidelity contact feedback mechanism is needed.
AI.method: The VISTA-Policy framework comprises three components: (1) a Physics-Aware Encoding Engine for real-time decoding of the Visual Deformation Field (VDF), a 3D displacement representation of a compliant gripper; (2) an Energy Aggregation Denoising Mechanism to isolate true interaction signals from noise; and (3) a Deformation-Augmented Policy Network that incorporates incremental gripper actions for precise closed-loop correction.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations on Cross-Scale Object Grasping, Cap Unscrewing, and Calligraphy Writing show VISTA-Policy outperforms the pure-vision 3D Diffusion Policy baseline and the tactile baseline. It also demonstrates substantial out-of-distribution generalization to unseen object scales and robustness against dynamic disturbances.
AI.conclusion: VDF-based visual deformation feedback offers a durable, cost-effective alternative to dedicated tactile sensors, enabling general-purpose fine-grained manipulation in unstructured environments without added hardware complexity.

title: Agentic Game Development as a Verifiable Trajectory Data Engine for Scaling World Models
summary: A common strategy for scaling world models is to train on more crawled video with more compute. We argue that this strategy is inefficient: scaling world models also requires a recursive data engine that offers grounded reward signals. The success of code agents illustrates why this matters. As code is executable, compilers and runtimes can provide high-quality rewards for Reinforcement Learning (RL) post-training of LLMs. By contrast, spatial generation still relies largely on fuzzy proxies such as CLIP scores. These signals are fuzzy and biased, making them hard to support RL post-training. Compared with these, game development provides a missing reward environment for spatial world models. A scene encoded by a game engine is an executable world specification: the engine can efficiently check collision, physics, navigability and bounded playability, while the developer provides the global verification signal by judging whether the scene should be accepted. Game development also provides real-world long-horizon trajectory data for RL post-training. We therefore propose Reinforcement Learning with Human-Engine Verification (RLHEV), a post-training paradigm that combines dense engine signals with implicit human acceptance feedback from the development process.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes RLHEV (Reinforcement Learning with Human-Engine Verification), a post-training paradigm for spatial world models that leverages game engines as grounded reward environments. Unlike scaling on crawled video data, game engines provide executable world specifications with dense reward signals (collision, physics, navigability, playability checkable) plus implicit human acceptance feedback from the development process.
AI.motivation: Scaling world models by simply training on more crawled video with more compute is inefficient. Unlike code agents that benefit from executable compilers/runtimes providing high-quality RL rewards, spatial generation relies on fuzzy proxies like CLIP scores that are hard to support RL post-training. There is a missing grounded reward environment for spatial world models.
AI.method: RLHEV combines two signal sources for RL post-training: (1) dense engine-based signals from game engines that efficiently check collision, physics, navigability, and bounded playability—treating a scene as an executable world specification; and (2) implicit human acceptance feedback derived from the real-world long-horizon trajectory data of the game development process, where the developer's judgment serves as a global verification signal.
AI.result: The paper proposes the RLHEV paradigm leveraging game development as a missing reward environment; specific experimental results are not presented in the abstract as this constitutes a proposal/framework argument.
AI.conclusion: Game development provides principled grounded rewards for spatial world models, enabling RL post-training through a recursive data engine that combines dense engine verification with implicit human feedback—analogous to the compiler/runtime rewards that made code agent RL successful.

title: Low-Resolution Perception for Robotic Packing
comment: 6 pages, 5 figures. Accepted to IFAC World Congress 2026
summary: This work tackles the problem of scalable perception for robotic packing with low-cost, low-resolution depth sensing. We propose a framework where reconstruction cues drive next-view selection and grasp evidence updates a per-object stability estimate, jointly deciding what to acquire next and when to grasp. During the reconstruction, a low-resolution Next Best View (NBV) strategy explicitly avoids redundant views while preserving task-relevant geometry. We validate the approach in two steps: (i) an ablation study of the utility function under very low resolution, and (ii) a full end-to-end evaluation across policies, showing how low-resolution perception is a practical, scalable option for robotic packing.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a scalable perception framework for robotic packing using low-cost, low-resolution depth sensing. The framework uses reconstruction cues to drive next-view selection and grasp evidence to update per-object stability estimates, jointly deciding what to acquire next and when to grasp. A low-resolution Next Best View (NBV) strategy avoids redundant views while preserving task-relevant geometry. Validation includes an ablation study of the utility function under very low resolution and a full end-to-end evaluation across policies demonstrating that low-resolution perception is a practical, scalable option for robotic packing.
AI.motivation: The work addresses the challenge of scalable perception for robotic packing, specifically aiming to make perception practical and scalable by leveraging low-cost, low-resolution depth sensors rather than expensive high-resolution hardware.
AI.method: The proposed framework integrates two key components: (1) reconstruction cues that drive next-view selection via a low-resolution Next Best View (NBV) strategy which avoids redundant views while preserving task-relevant geometry, and (2) grasp evidence that updates a per-object stability estimate. These jointly determine what to acquire next and when to grasp.
AI.result: Validation was conducted in two steps: an ablation study of the utility function under very low resolution, and a full end-to-end evaluation across policies. Results demonstrate that low-resolution perception is a practical, scalable option for robotic packing.
AI.conclusion: Low-resolution depth sensing combined with a reconstruction-guided NBV strategy and per-object stability estimates via grasp evidence provides a practical and scalable perception solution for robotic packing, achieving effective performance without the need for high-resolution sensors.

title: Using profiles of cognitive capability to assess AI suitability for workplace tasks
summary: Organisations deploying AI face a scoping problem: which tasks can be automated, which should remain with humans, and which are best shared between the two. Aggregate benchmark scores provide little insight into where systems will succeed or fail in practice, while human judgements of model capabilities quickly become outdated. We introduce a pipeline that profiles agents and tasks using a shared set of core cognitive capabilities. Cognitive capability profiling infers an agent's capabilities from performance on a benchmark battery annotated for the cognitive demands of each item. Task requirements weighting elicits from domain experts the relative importance of these same capabilities for their work. As both use a common set of cognitive dimensions, they can be updated independently as models and roles change, and combined to estimate AI suitability at the level of a domain, organisation, role, or individual duty. We validate capability recovery on synthetic agents, profile six AI systems, and elicit task requirements from 410 employees across six occupational domains. AI systems differed more across cognitive dimensions than across model families, while workplace activities converged on a shared cognitive core. The resulting scores provide a comparative scoping tool for identifying promising candidates for piloting and areas where current systems are unlikely to be well suited. We discuss extending the framework to profile human workers alongside AI systems, moving from AI suitability towards human-machine task allocation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a cognitive capability profiling pipeline to address the scoping problem of AI deployment—which tasks to automate, share, or keep human. It profiles agents via a benchmark battery annotated for cognitive demands and elicits task requirement weights from domain experts, both using a shared set of cognitive dimensions. Validated on synthetic agents, six AI systems, and 410 employees across six domains, it provides a comparative tool for AI suitability and task allocation.
AI.motivation: Organisations face a scoping problem in AI deployment because aggregate benchmark scores fail to predict real-world success or failure, and human judgements of model capabilities rapidly become outdated. There is a need for a more granular, updatable method to determine which tasks can be automated, which should stay with humans, and which are best shared.
AI.method: The pipeline comprises two components: (1) cognitive capability profiling, which infers an agent's capabilities from performance on a benchmark battery annotated for cognitive demands per item; and (2) task requirements weighting, which elicits from domain experts the relative importance of shared cognitive capabilities for their work. Both use a common set of cognitive dimensions, enabling independent updates and combination to estimate AI suitability at domain, organisation, role, or duty levels.
AI.result: Capability recovery was validated on synthetic agents. Six AI systems were profiled and task requirements were elicited from 410 employees across six occupational domains. AI systems differed more across cognitive dimensions than across model families, while workplace activities converged on a shared cognitive core. The resulting scores serve as a comparative scoping tool for identifying piloting candidates and areas of poor system fit.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a comparative scoping tool for AI deployment decisions. The authors propose extending it to profile human workers alongside AI systems, moving from AI suitability assessment towards human-machine task allocation.

title: A Statistical Audit of Physical AI Benchmark Redundancy
summary: Physical AI models are evaluated on suites of benchmarks that differ across model reports, leaving the model-by-benchmark matrix sparse and the relationship between benchmarks unmeasured. We construct a matrix of 51 models on 12 physical AI benchmarks, selected from a registry of 51 benchmarks and 152 models by reporting density, combining scores from model cards and benchmark papers with our own evaluation runs under each benchmark's official protocol. We measure how much information the benchmarks share and show quantitative evidence of Redundancy. Redundancy affects reported rankings: collapsing the two substitute pairs into single columns moves 22 of 51 models by three or more places under an equally weighted average. We then select benchmarks greedily under a utility combining score dispersion with variance not explained by the already-selected set, and obtain a four-benchmark subset retaining 78.5\% of the utility of all 12, on which we fit a Bradley--Terry ranking. The procedure requires only benchmark-level scores with sufficient overlap and is not specific to physical AI.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs a benchmark-score matrix of 51 models across 12 physical AI benchmarks, demonstrates quantitative evidence of benchmark redundancy that shifts model rankings, and proposes a greedy benchmark-selection procedure that retains 78.5% of utility with only 4 benchmarks, on which a Bradley–Terry ranking is fitted.
AI.motivation: Physical AI models are evaluated on inconsistent benchmark suites across reports, resulting in a sparse model-by-benchmark matrix and an unmeasured relationship between benchmarks. This makes cross-model comparison and benchmark interpretation unreliable.
AI.method: The authors assemble a 51-model × 12-benchmark matrix from a registry of 51 benchmarks and 152 models, filling gaps with their own evaluation runs under official protocols. They quantify shared information between benchmarks, demonstrate redundancy's effect on rankings by collapsing substitute pairs, and greedily select benchmarks using a utility combining score dispersion with residual unexplained variance, then fit a Bradley–Terry model on the selected subset.
AI.result: Two substitute benchmark pairs were identified; collapsing them moves 22 of 51 models by three or more places under equal-weighted averaging. A four-benchmark subset retains 78.5% of the full 12-benchmark utility, and a Bradley–Terry ranking is derived on it.
AI.conclusion: Benchmark redundancy is measurable and materially affects reported rankings. A lightweight, model-agnostic greedy selection procedure can reduce benchmark suites substantially while preserving ranking utility, with applicability beyond physical AI.

title: Narcissus: Program Synthesis Using Context-Aware LLM Approximations
summary: Large language models (LLMs) excel at programming, but not when the task fixes the target language: prompted with a grammar rare in their training data, their programs usually break the grammar or fail the given specification. Enumerative synthesizers search the space of syntactically correct programs systematically guided by LLMs; the state of the art guides them by approximating LLM proposals into rule frequencies, which loses where each construct belongs and prunes every rule the proposals miss, exactly when the proposals are wrong. We present Narcissus, a synthesizer that keeps the proposals as syntax trees and scores each expansion of a candidate program in its context: does a proposal with the same surrounding structure continue the same way, and does the expansion rebuild a fragment the proposals repeat? A regularization term keeps every rule reachable, so wrong proposals delay the solution but cannot hide it. Across five domains and two search backends, Narcissus beats static guidance at every budget and consistently outperforms re-prompting the LLM to fix its own proposals; it reaches proposal-like programs an order of magnitude sooner and solves $40\%$ of ARC tasks where the raw proposals solve $13\%$, all without a single LLM call during search.

AI.tldr: Narcissus is a program synthesizer that bridges LLMs and enumerative search by using LLM proposals as syntax trees to guide search expansion contextually, rather than approximating them into rule frequencies. It achieves significant improvements over static guidance and LLM re-prompting across five domains and two search backends, requiring no LLM calls during search.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle to generate programs in low-resource grammars (rare in training data), producing grammatically invalid or spec-violating code. Existing LLM-guided enumerative synthesizers convert LLM proposals into rule frequencies, which loses structural context and aggressively prunes rules the proposals miss—exactly when proposals are wrong, hiding correct solutions.
AI.method: Narcissus keeps LLM proposals as syntax trees and scores each expansion choice in its context: (1) whether a proposal with the same surrounding structure continues the same way, and (2) whether the expansion rebuilds a fragment that proposals repeat. A regularization term ensures every grammar rule remains reachable, so incorrect proposals slow search but cannot eliminate correct solutions. It combines this with two different search backends.
AI.result: Across five domains and two search backends, Narcissus outperforms static guidance at every budget and consistently beats re-prompting the LLM to fix its own proposals. It reaches proposal-like programs an order of magnitude faster and solves 40% of ARC tasks where raw LLM proposals solve only 13%, all without any LLM calls during search.
AI.conclusion: Contextual, syntax-tree-based guidance that preserves grammatical structure and keeps all rules reachable is a superior strategy for LLM-guided program synthesis than rule-frequency approximations, and it eliminates the need for expensive iterative LLM re-prompting during search.

title: DESCENT: Directed Edge Scene Encoding for Airport Surface Movement Prediction
summary: Advanced automation is a key technology for enhancing the safety of ground operations amidst the increasing density of commercial air traffic.
